solutions.latex:
The mean is the midpoint of the bounds.

$$\mu = \dfrac{145 + 25}{2} = 85$$

Since $99.7\%$ of the area is bounded, the empirical rule gives three standard deviations from the mean.

$$\begin{aligned} \sigma &= \dfrac{85 - 25}{3} = 20 \\ \text{Var}(X) &= \sigma^2 = 20^2 = 400 \end{aligned}$$

So $\mu = 85$ and $\text{Var}(X) = 400$.

parts.latex: Prove that $\dfrac{\sin A}{1 + \cos A} + \dfrac{1 + \cos A}{\sin A} = 2\operatorname{cosec} A$.

solutions.latex:
Combine the fractions over the common denominator $\sin A(1 + \cos A)$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\sin A}{1 + \cos A} + \dfrac{1 + \cos A}{\sin A} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2 A}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} + \dfrac{(1 + \cos A)^2}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2 A + 1 + 2\cos A + \cos^2 A}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} \\ &= \dfrac{2 + 2\cos A}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} &&(\text{since } \sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1) \\ &= \dfrac{2(1 + \cos A)}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\sin A} \\ &= 2\operatorname{cosec} A \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Combines the fractions together and applies trigonometric identities to assist with the proof, or equivalent merit
Combines the fractions together, or equivalent merit

An airport scanner screens bags for prohibited items. An alarm is supposed to be triggered when a prohibited item is detected.

On a given day, $5\%$ of bags contain prohibited items. If a bag contains prohibited items, there is a $95\%$ chance that it triggers the alarm. If a bag does not contain prohibited items, there is a $2\%$ chance that it triggers the alarm.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{277_q14_s1}

The completed branches are $\dfrac{95}{100}$ and $\dfrac{5}{100}$ (alarm and no alarm, given a prohibited item) and $\dfrac{2}{100}$ and $\dfrac{98}{100}$ (alarm and no alarm, given no prohibited item).
criteria: Provides at least TWO correct values

From prohibited: alarm $\dfrac{95}{100}$, no alarm $\dfrac{5}{100}$. From not prohibited: alarm $\dfrac{2}{100}$, no alarm $\dfrac{98}{100}$. Note: the part (b) source working uses $\frac{95}{100}\times\frac{2}{100}$ for the not-prohibited-and-alarm path, which should be $\frac{95}{100}\times\frac{2}{100}$ with 95/100 as P(not prohibited); this is consistent.

solutions.latex:
Using the conditional probability formula,

$$P(\text{prohibited} \mid \text{alarm}) = \dfrac{P(\text{prohibited} \cap \text{alarm})}{P(\text{alarm})}$$

From the tree,

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{prohibited} \mid \text{alarm}) &= \dfrac{\frac{5}{100} \times \frac{95}{100}}{\frac{5}{100} \times \frac{95}{100} + \frac{95}{100} \times \frac{2}{100}} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{7} \end{aligned}$$

3324.stem:
The heights of 30 mothers and daughters were recorded. The results are shown in the scatterplot. The least-squares regression line on the scatterplot passes through the point $(180, 184)$.

\exfigure{277_q15_1}

figures.cap: scatterplot of daughter's height against mother's height with least-squares line through (180, 184)

parts.latex:
Katarina calculated that the correlation coefficient for this data set is $r = -2.5$.

Without calculating the correlation coefficient, give TWO reasons why Katarina must be incorrect.
parts.note: Correlation coefficient (bivariate data) is not in 2024 Advanced

parts.latex:
The equation of the least-squares regression line for this data set is in the form

$$y = 0.8077x + A,$$

where $A$ is a constant. Katarina is 160 cm tall.

Use the equation of the least-squares regression line to estimate the height of Katarina's mother. Give your answer correct to the nearest whole number.
parts.note: Least-squares regression line prediction is not in 2024 Advanced

solutions.latex:
A correlation coefficient satisfies $-1 \le r \le 1$, and $r = -2.5$ lies outside this restriction.

Also, the scatterplot shows a positive correlation, so $r$ should be positive, with $0 < r < 1$.

Hence Katarina is incorrect for these two reasons.

The line passes through $(180, 184)$, so substitute to find $A$.

$$\begin{aligned} 184 &= 0.8077(180) + A \\ 184 &= 145.386 + A \\ A &= 38.614 \end{aligned}$$

So $y = 0.8077x + 38.614$. Katarina is 160 cm tall, so $y = 160$.

$$\begin{aligned} 160 &= 0.8077x + 38.614 \\ x &\approx 150.285 \end{aligned}$$

Katarina's mother is approximately 150 cm tall.

parts.latex: Evaluate $f'(\pi)$ given that $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2}{\cos x}$.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right) = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u &= x^2 & v &= \cos x \\ u' &= 2x & v' &= -\sin x \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{(\cos x)(2x) - (x^2)(-\sin x)}{\cos^2 x} \\ &= \dfrac{x(2\cos x + x\sin x)}{\cos^2 x} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'(\pi) &= \dfrac{\pi(2\cos\pi + \pi\sin\pi)}{\cos^2\pi} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi(-2 + 0)}{(-1)^2} \\ &= -2\pi \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the quotient rule to differentiate $f(x)$

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1 + \ln x$.
Hence, or otherwise, evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^e \ln x\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv) = u'v + uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u &= x & v &= \ln x \\ u' &= 1 & v' &= \dfrac{1}{x} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= (1)(\ln x) + (x)\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) \\ &= 1 + \ln x \end{aligned}$$

From part (a), $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1 + \ln x$. By the fundamental theorem of calculus,

$$\displaystyle \int_1^e (1 + \ln x)\,dx = \Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^e$$

Split the left side and rearrange.

$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^e \ln x\,dx &= \Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^e - \int_1^e 1\,dx \\ &= \Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^e - \Big[x\Big]_1^e \\ &= (e\ln e - 1\ln 1) - (e - 1) \\ &= e - (e - 1) \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the fundamental theorem of calculus to the solution found in part (a)

parts.latex:
A basketball player shoots a ball from a height of 2 metres into a hoop 14 metres away. The hoop 3 metres from the ground. After moving 5 metres horizontally, the ball reaches a height of 4 metres from the ground. This information is shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{277_q20_1}

The path of the ball can be modelled by the quadratic function

$$y = ax^2 + bx + c,$$

where $y$ represents the height of the ball from the ground, $x$ is the horizontal displacement from the basketball player, and $a$, $b$ and $c$ are constants.

Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$ that best model the path of the ball.

solutions.latex:
Place the origin at the ground below the player. The ball passes through $(0, 2)$, $(5, 4)$ and $(14, 3)$.

\exfigure{277_q20_s1}

Substituting $(0, 2)$ gives $c = 2$, so $y = ax^2 + bx + 2$.

Substituting $(5, 4)$:

$$\begin{aligned} 4 &= 25a + 5b + 2 \\ 2 &= 25a + 5b \\ a &= \dfrac{2 - 5b}{25} && (1) \end{aligned}$$

Substituting $(14, 3)$:

$$1 = 196a + 14b \qquad (2)$$

Substituting (1) into (2):

$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= 196\left(\dfrac{2 - 5b}{25}\right) + 14b \\ 25 &= 392 - 980b + 350b \\ b &= \dfrac{367}{630} \end{aligned}$$

Then

$$a = \dfrac{2 - 5\left(\frac{367}{630}\right)}{25} = -\dfrac{23}{630}$$

$$\therefore\ a = -\dfrac{23}{630},\ b = \dfrac{367}{630},\ c = 2$$
criteria: Finds the value of $c$ and develops simultaneous equations to solve for $a$ and $b$

parts.latex: If the company chooses model A, show that the company would make a revenue of $\$292\,820$ in 2025.
If the company chooses model B, find the value of $M$ such that the company's revenue is $\$292\,820$ in 2025.

solutions.latex:
Method 1: Model A is a geometric sequence, since each year's revenue is $1.1$ times the previous year's.

Here $a = 200\,000$ and $r = \dfrac{110}{100} = 1.1$, so
$$T_n = 200\,000(1.1)^{n-1}$$
For 2025, $n = 5$ (2021 is $n=1$).
$$\begin{aligned} T_5 &= 200\,000(1.1)^{5-1} \\ &= 292\,820 \end{aligned}$$
Method 2: Using the compound growth formula with 4 years of growth,
$$\begin{aligned} A &= P(1 + r)^n \\ &= 200\,000(1 + 0.1)^4 \\ &= 292\,820 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the revenue in 2025 is } \$292\,820$$
criteria: Finds the general term $T_n$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Model B adds a fixed amount each year, so it is an arithmetic sequence with $a = 200\,000$ and $d = M$.
$$T_n = 200\,000 + (n - 1)M$$
For 2025, $n = 5$ and $T_5 = 292\,820$.
$$\begin{aligned} 292\,820 &= 200\,000 + (5 - 1)M \\ 92\,820 &= 4M \\ M &= 23\,205 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ M = \$23\,205$$
criteria: Finds the general term $T_n$, or equivalent merit

A hiker starts from point $P$ and walks 100 metres along a straight path to the north-east, arriving at point $Q$. A peak is located at point $R$, which is directly above point $X$. From point $P$, the angle of elevation to peak $R$ is $10^\circ$. At point $Q$, the angle of elevation to the peak is $5^\circ$.

\exfigure{277_q23_1}

parts.latex: Show that $XP = h\cot 10^\circ$ and find a similar expression for $XQ$.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (peak above level ground seen from two points)

parts.latex: Hence, find the value of $h$. Give your answer correct to the nearest metre.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (peak above level ground seen from two points)

solutions.latex:
$\triangle RPX$ is right-angled at $X$, so using the tangent ratio:
$$\tan 10^\circ = \dfrac{RX}{XP} = \dfrac{h}{XP}$$
$$XP = \dfrac{h}{\tan 10^\circ} = h\cot 10^\circ$$
$\triangle RQX$ is right-angled at $X$, so likewise:
$$\tan 5^\circ = \dfrac{h}{XQ}$$
$$XQ = h\cot 5^\circ$$
criteria: Shows that $XP = h\cot 10^\circ$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$\triangle XPQ$ is right-angled at $X$, since $PX \perp QX$ (the paths run NW and NE). Applying Pythagoras' theorem with $PQ = 100$:
$$XP^2 + PQ^2 = XQ^2$$
Substituting $XP = h\cot 10^\circ$ and $XQ = h\cot 5^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} h^2\cot^2 10^\circ + 10\,000 &= h^2\cot^2 5^\circ \\ 10\,000 &= h^2\left(\cot^2 5^\circ - \cot^2 10^\circ\right) \\ h &= \sqrt{\dfrac{10\,000}{\cot^2 5^\circ - \cot^2 10^\circ}} \\ &\approx 10 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h \approx 10 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Makes $h^2$ the subject, or equivalent merit
Applies Pythagoras' theorem to $\triangle XPQ$, or equivalent merit

3334.stem:
On a given day, the height of the water in a river is modelled by the function

$$h(t) = 5 + 3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right),$$

where $h$ is the height of the water, in metres, and $t$ is the time, in hours, after 12 am.

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of h(t) on [0,24]

parts.latex: What is the height of the water at 12 am?
Sketch the graph of $h(t) = 5 + 3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)$ in the domain $[0, 24]$.

A family decides to go on a picnic by the river from 12 pm to 2 pm. It is only safe to swim in the river if the height of the water is less than 4 metres.

When is the earliest time the family can swim in the river after 12 pm? Give your answer correct to the nearest minute.

solutions.latex:
The height at 12 am is found by putting $t = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} h(0) &= 5 + 3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} \times 0\right) \\ &= 5 + 3\sin 0 \\ &= 5 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

The period of $\sin nt$ is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$, here with $n = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
$$T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{4}} = 8$$
The amplitude is $3$ and the centre line is $h = 5$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{maximum} &= 5 + 3 = 8 \\ \text{minimum} &= 5 - 3 = 2 \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{277_q24_s1}
criteria: Any TWO of: the period, the maximum and minimum values, the correct graph shape, or equivalent merit
Any ONE of these, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Figure 277_q24_s1 is referenced in the source; sketch_id on the item is 277_q24_s2. Graph should show $h = 5 + 3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)$ on $[0,24]$: starts at $(0,5)$, period $8$, max $8$ at $t = 2, 10, 18$, min $2$ at $t = 6, 14, 22$.

solutions.latex:
The water is safe to swim in when $h < 4$, so first solve $h = 4$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4 &= 5 + 3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}t\right) \\ -\dfrac{1}{3} &= \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}t\right) \end{aligned}$$
The reference angle is $\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) \approx 0.3398$, and sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants.
$$\dfrac{\pi}{4}t = \pi + 0.3398,\ 2\pi - 0.3398,\ 3\pi + 0.3398,\ 4\pi - 0.3398,\ \ldots$$
$$t \approx 4.433,\ 7.567,\ 12.43,\ 15.57,\ \ldots \text{ hours}$$
The family is at the river from $t = 12$ to $t = 14$, so $t = 12.43$ is the first time in that period when $h = 4$, after which $h < 4$.

$12.43$ hours is $12$ hours $26$ minutes.
$$\therefore\ \text{the earliest time is } 12{:}26 \text{ pm}$$
criteria: Solves the trigonometric equation for possible values of $t$, or equivalent merit
Substitutes $h = 4$ to develop a trigonometric equation, or equivalent merit

The asymptote $y = 0$ maps to $y = 1$.

3336.stem:
Consider the function $y = \dfrac{2x}{e^x}$.

It is known that as $x \to \infty$, $y \to 0$ and as $x \to -\infty = y \to \infty$

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y = 2x/e^x

parts.latex: Find the $x$- and $y$-intercepts.
Find and classify any turning points on $y = \dfrac{2x}{e^x}$.
Show that a point of inflection occurs at $\left(2, \dfrac{4}{e^2}\right)$.
Sketch the graph of $y = \dfrac{2x}{e^x}$, labelling all important features.

solutions.latex:
For the $x$-intercept, let $y = 0$.
$$0 = \dfrac{2x}{e^x}$$
so $x = 0$, and the $x$-intercept is $(0, 0)$.

For the $y$-intercept, let $x = 0$.
$$y = \dfrac{2(0)}{e^0} = 0$$
so the $y$-intercept is $(0, 0)$.

$$\therefore\ y = \dfrac{2x}{e^x} \text{ has one intercept, at the origin}$$

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right) = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u &= 2x & v &= e^x \\ u' &= 2 & v' &= e^x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{(e^x)(2) - (2x)(e^x)}{(e^x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{2e^x(1 - x)}{e^{2x}} \\ &= \dfrac{2(1 - x)}{e^x} \end{aligned}$$
For stationary points $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$, so $1 - x = 0$ and $x = 1$.
$$y = \dfrac{2(1)}{e^1} = \dfrac{2}{e}$$
The sign of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ is decided by $1 - x$ (as $e^x > 0$), so test either side of $x = 1$.

\extable{Ts4790_1}

The gradient changes from positive to negative.
$$\therefore\ \left(1, \dfrac{2}{e}\right) \text{ is a maximum turning point}$$
criteria: Finds the stationary point $\left(1, \dfrac{2}{e}\right)$, or equivalent merit
Finds the derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{2(1 - x)}{e^x}$ using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right) = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u &= 1 - x & v &= e^x \\ u' &= -1 & v' &= e^x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &= 2\left[\dfrac{(e^x)(-1) - (1 - x)(e^x)}{e^{2x}}\right] \\ &= 2\left(\dfrac{xe^x - 2e^x}{e^{2x}}\right) \\ &= 2\left(\dfrac{x - 2}{e^x}\right) \end{aligned}$$
For a possible point of inflection $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 0$, so $x - 2 = 0$ and $x = 2$.
$$y = \dfrac{2(2)}{e^2} = \dfrac{4}{e^2}$$
The sign of $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ is decided by $x - 2$, so test either side of $x = 2$.

\extable{Ts4791_1}

There is a change in concavity.
$$\therefore\ \left(2, \dfrac{4}{e^2}\right) \text{ is a point of inflection}$$
criteria: Finds that a possible point of inflection occurs at $\left(2, \dfrac{4}{e^2}\right)$, or equivalent merit
Finds the second derivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The time, in minutes, between the arrival of customers at an Automated Teller Machine (ATM) is represented by the variable, $t$, which is a continuous random variable modelled by the probability density function

$$f(t) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{3}e^{-\frac{t}{3}} & t \ge 0 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

Find the median time between the arrival of customers at the ATM. Give your answer correct to the nearest minute.

solutions.latex:
Let $F(x)$ be the cumulative distribution function.
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_0^x \dfrac{1}{3}e^{-\frac{t}{3}}\,dt \\ &= \left[-e^{-\frac{t}{3}}\right]_0^x \\ &= -\left(e^{-\frac{x}{3}} - 1\right) \\ &= 1 - e^{-\frac{x}{3}} \end{aligned}$$
The median is the value of $x$ with $F(x) = 0.5$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.5 &= 1 - e^{-\frac{x}{3}} \\ e^{-\frac{x}{3}} &= 0.5 \\ -\dfrac{x}{3} &= \ln 0.5 \\ x &= -3\ln 0.5 \\ &= 2.079\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the median time is } 2 \text{ minutes}$$
criteria: Makes valid progress in solving $F(x) = 0.5$ for the median time, or equivalent merit
Finds the cumulative distribution function, or equivalent merit

3338.stem:
A particle moves in a straight line such that its displacement is given by the function

$$x = 2 - \dfrac{3}{t + 1},$$

where $x$ is the particle's displacement from the origin, in metres, and $t$ is the time, in seconds.

parts.latex: What is the initial displacement of the particle?
Find the expressions for the velocity and acceleration of the particle in terms of $t$.
As $t$ increases indefinitely, describe the motion of the particle with reference to its displacement and velocity.

solutions.latex:
Since $2 - \dfrac{3}{t + 1} = \dfrac{2t - 1}{t + 1}$, the displacement can be written $x = \dfrac{2t - 1}{t + 1}$.

The initial displacement is at $t = 0$.
$$x = \dfrac{2(0) - 1}{0 + 1} = -1$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is initially } 1 \text{ metre to the left of the origin}$$

Rewrite the displacement with a negative power, then differentiate.
$$x = 2 - 3(t + 1)^{-1}$$
$$v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 3(t + 1)^{-2} = \dfrac{3}{(t + 1)^2}$$
$$a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = -6(t + 1)^{-3} = -\dfrac{6}{(t + 1)^3}$$
criteria: Finds the expression for $v$ OR $a$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
As $t \to \infty$, $\dfrac{3}{t + 1} \to 0$, so $x \to 2 - 0 = 2$.

The particle approaches $x = 2$ m.

As $t \to \infty$, $v = \dfrac{3}{(t+1)^2} \to 0$.

The particle's velocity decreases towards $0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the particle approaches } x = 2 \text{ m with decreasing speed}$$
criteria: Describes the particle's displacement OR velocity as $t \to \infty$, or equivalent merit

3339.stem:
An equilateral triangle has a perimeter of $p$ cm. The midpoints of each side are connected to form another triangle. This pattern can continue for an infinite number of times, as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{277_q29_1}

figures.cap: nested equilateral triangles formed by joining midpoints

parts.latex: Show that the perimeter of the $n$th triangle is $\dfrac{p}{2^{n-1}}$.
Find an expression in terms of $p$ that represents the total perimeter of all the triangles.

solutions.latex:
Joining the midpoints of an equilateral triangle gives a similar triangle with half the side length, so half the perimeter.

The perimeters form a geometric sequence with $a = p$ and $r = \dfrac{1}{2}$. Let $p_n$ be the perimeter of the $n$th triangle.
$$\begin{aligned} p_n &= ar^{n-1} \\ &= p\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-1} \\ &= p\left(\dfrac{1^{n-1}}{2^{n-1}}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{p}{2^{n-1}} \end{aligned}$$
since $1^{n-1} = 1$.
criteria: Finds an expression for $p_n$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The total perimeter is the sum to infinity of the GP, which exists as $|r| = \dfrac{1}{2} < 1$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1 - r} \\ &= \dfrac{p}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{p}{\frac{1}{2}} \\ &= 2p \end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: dartboard with radii 2 cm, 5 cm, 20 cm

parts.latex:
Paula, who is new to playing darts, throws a dart so that it lands somewhere on the board.

Show that the probability that Paula's dart will land in the centre circle is $\dfrac{1}{100}$.

Paula has two attempts at throwing a dart at the board. On one of her attempts, Paula's dart lands in the centre circle. On another attempt, her dart lands in the outer section.

Show that the probability that this occurs, in any order, is $\dfrac{3}{160}$.

Let $X$ be a discrete random variable that represents the number of points scored after two attempts at throwing a dart at the board. The probability distribution table is shown.

\extable{277_q30_t2}

An amateur dart player is throwing two darts to achieve a score. Assume the probability distribution table models the amateur player's likelihood of landing a dart in a specific section.

Calculate the expected value of the probability distribution.
Calculate the standard deviation of the probability distribution. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

solutions.latex:
The probability is the ratio of the areas of the centre circle and the whole board.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{centre}) &= \dfrac{\pi(2)^2}{\pi(20)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{400} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{100} \end{aligned}$$

The outer section is the board minus the circle of radius $5$.
$$P(\text{outer}) = \dfrac{\pi(20)^2 - \pi(5)^2}{\pi(20)^2} = \dfrac{15}{16}$$
The two attempts can occur in either order, so multiply by $2$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{centre and outer, any order}) &= 2 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{100} \times \dfrac{\pi(20)^2 - \pi(5)^2}{\pi(20)^2}\right) \\ &= 2 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{100} \times \dfrac{15}{16}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{3}{160} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the probability of a dart landing in the outer section, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the expected value formula $E(X) = \sum x\,p(x)$ with the values from the table:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= 10\left(\dfrac{225}{256}\right) + 25\left(\dfrac{63}{640}\right) + 40\left(\dfrac{441}{160\,000}\right) \\ &\quad + 105\left(\dfrac{3}{160}\right) + 120\left(\dfrac{21}{20\,000}\right) + 200\left(\dfrac{1}{10\,000}\right) \\ &= 13.475 \end{aligned}$$

First find the values of $x^2 p(x)$.

\extable{Ts4802_1}

Using $\text{Var}(X) = \sum x^2 p(x) - \mu^2$ with $\mu = 13.475$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X) &= \dfrac{5625}{64} + \dfrac{7875}{128} + \dfrac{441}{100} + \dfrac{6615}{32} + \dfrac{378}{25} + 4 - 13.475^2 \\ &= 198.087\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sigma &= \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)} \\ &= \sqrt{198.087\ldots} \\ &\approx 14.07 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \sigma \approx 14.07 \text{ (to two decimal places)}$$
criteria: Provides the correct value for $\text{Var}(X)$, or equivalent merit
Finds the values for the $x^2 p(x)$ column, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that the length of the whiteboard, $L$, is $\dfrac{3}{\cos\theta} + \dfrac{4}{\sin\theta}$.
What is the maximum possible length of the whiteboard that can be carried around the corner?

solutions.latex:
Divide the whiteboard into two parts, $L_1$ and $L_2$, one in each corridor.

\exfigure{277_q31_s1}

In the right-angled triangle containing $L_1$ (width $3$), using the cosine ratio:
$$\cos\theta = \dfrac{3}{L_1}, \quad L_1 = \dfrac{3}{\cos\theta}$$
In the right-angled triangle containing $L_2$ (width $4$), using the sine ratio:
$$\sin\theta = \dfrac{4}{L_2}, \quad L_2 = \dfrac{4}{\sin\theta}$$
$$\therefore\ L = L_1 + L_2 = \dfrac{3}{\cos\theta} + \dfrac{4}{\sin\theta}$$
criteria: Makes valid progress to show the expression for $L$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The whiteboard forms an angle $0^\circ < \theta < 90^\circ$. As it enters from the bottom corridor, $\theta$ starts towards $90^\circ$, then decreases towards $0^\circ$ as it moves around the corner.

Entering the corridors:

\exfigure{277_q31_s2}

Moving around the corner:

\exfigure{277_q31_s3}

When $\theta$ is close to either bound, $L \to \infty$ in $L = \dfrac{3}{\cos\theta} + \dfrac{4}{\sin\theta}$, but then the whiteboard is too long to make it around the corner.

\exfigure{277_q31_s4}

The whiteboard turning the corner is limited by the shortest possible value of $L$, so the angle that minimises $L$ must be found.

Write
$$L = \dfrac{3}{\cos\theta} + \dfrac{4}{\sin\theta} = 3(\cos\theta)^{-1} + 4(\sin\theta)^{-1}$$
Differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dL}{d\theta} &= -3(\cos\theta)^{-2}(-\sin\theta) - 4(\sin\theta)^{-2}(\cos\theta) \\ &= \dfrac{3\sin\theta}{\cos^2\theta} - \dfrac{4\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{3\sin^3\theta - 4\cos^3\theta}{\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta} \end{aligned}$$
For stationary points $\dfrac{dL}{d\theta} = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3\sin^3\theta &= 4\cos^3\theta \\ \tan^3\theta &= \dfrac{4}{3} \\ \theta &= \tan^{-1}\left[\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}\right] \\ &= 0.833\ldots \text{ rad} \\ &= 47.74^\circ \end{aligned}$$
The sign of $\dfrac{dL}{d\theta}$ is decided by the numerator $3\sin^3\theta - 4\cos^3\theta$ (the denominator is positive), so test either side of $\theta = 47.74^\circ$.

\extable{Ts4804_1}

The gradient changes from negative to positive.

Hence $\theta = 47.74^\circ$ is a minimum turning point. When $\theta = 47.74^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} L &= \dfrac{3}{\cos 47.74^\circ} + \dfrac{4}{\sin 47.74^\circ} \\ &\approx 9.86 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the maximum possible length of the whiteboard is } 9.86 \text{ metres}$$
criteria: Tests AND shows that the stationary point is a minimum turning point, or equivalent merit
Shows that $\theta = 47.74^\circ$ is a stationary point, or equivalent merit
Finds an expression for $\dfrac{dL}{d\theta}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: A circle has the equation $(x+3)^2+(y-4)^2=d$. What is the value of $d$ such that the $x$-axis is a tangent to the circle?

solutions.latex:
The circle has centre $(-3,4)$ and radius $r=\sqrt{d}$.

The $x$-axis is a tangent when the distance from the centre to the $x$-axis equals the radius.

The centre is $4$ units above the $x$-axis, so
$$\begin{aligned} r &= 4 \\ d &= r^2 = 16 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the correct option is D, $d=16$.

parts.latex: What is the domain of the function $f(x)=\ln(3-x)+\sqrt{5x-4}$?

solutions.latex:
Each part of the function must be defined.

The logarithm needs a positive argument:
$$3-x>0 \quad\text{so}\quad x<3$$
The square root needs a non-negative argument:
$$5x-4\ge 0 \quad\text{so}\quad x\ge \dfrac{4}{5}$$
Combining, the domain is $\dfrac{4}{5}\le x<3$, that is $x\in\left[\dfrac{4}{5},3\right)$.

Hence the correct option is C.

parts.latex: A particle, initially $3$ m to the right of the origin has a velocity given by $v=(7-3t)$ ms$^{-1}$. What is an expression for the the displacement of the particle?

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the integral of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int (7-3t)\,dt \\ &= 7t-\dfrac{3t^2}{2}+C \end{aligned}$$
Initially ($t=0$) the particle is $3$ m to the right of the origin, so $x=3$ when $t=0$:
$$3=0-0+C \quad\text{so}\quad C=3$$
Hence $x=7t-\dfrac{3t^2}{2}+3$, which is option A.

parts.latex:
Consider the two sets $A=\{6,7,8\}$ and $B=\{11,12,13\}$. A number is randomly selected from each set.

What is the probability of selecting a number from each set that has a sum equal to or greater than 20?

solutions.latex:
There are $3\times3=9$ equally likely pairs.

The pairs with sum at least $20$ are:
$$(7,13),\ (8,12),\ (8,13)$$
The other pairs have sum at most $19$ (for example $6+13=19$ and $7+12=19$).
$$P(\text{sum}\ge 20)=\dfrac{3}{9}=\dfrac{1}{3}$$
Hence the correct option is C.

where $0\le x\le 2\pi$.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}4\cos x&=-2\sqrt{3}\\\cos x&=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
The reference angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants.
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6} \text{ or } \pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6}$$

parts.latex: Prove that $\dfrac{\sec\theta-\sec\theta\cos^4\theta}{1+\cos^2\theta}=\sin\theta\tan\theta$

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\sec\theta-\sec\theta\cos^4\theta}{1+\cos^2\theta}\\&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{\cos\theta}-\frac{\cos^4\theta}{\cos\theta}}{1+\cos^2\theta}\\&=\dfrac{1-\cos^4\theta}{\cos\theta\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right)}\\&=\dfrac{\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right)\left(1-\cos^2\theta\right)}{\cos\theta\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right)}\\&=\dfrac{1-\cos^2\theta}{\cos\theta}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta}\\&=\sin\theta\times\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\\&=\sin\theta\tan\theta\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Factorises the difference of squares and cancels, or equivalent merit
Writes as a single fraction in terms of $\cos\theta$, or equivalent merit

3359.stem:
A footpath on horizontal ground has two parallel edges. $CD$ is a vertical street sign pole of height $h$ metres which stands with its base $C$ on one edge of the footpath. $A$ and $B$ are two points on the other edge of the footpath such that $AB=7$ m and $\angle ACB=60^\circ$. From $A$ and $B$, the angles of elevation to the top of the pole at $D$ are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ respectively.

\exfigure{1334_q18_1}

figures.cap: pole CD of height h at C on one footpath edge; A, B on the other edge, AB = 7 m, width w, angles 60, 30, 60

parts.latex: Show that the exact height of the flagpole is $h=\sqrt{21}$ metres.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (pole seen from two points on level ground): now Year 11 Extension 1, not Advanced.

parts.latex: By considering the area of $\triangle ABC$, find the exact width $w$ of the footpath.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry question (whole question removed): now Year 11 Extension 1, not Advanced.

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle BCD$, using $\tan 60^\circ=\dfrac{h}{CB}$:
$$CB=\dfrac{h}{\tan 60^\circ}=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}$$
In $\triangle ACD$, using $\tan 30^\circ=\dfrac{h}{CA}$:
$$CA=\dfrac{h}{\tan30^\circ}=\sqrt{3}h$$
Apply the cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$:
$$AB^2=CB^2+CA^2-2(CB)(CA)\cos 60^\circ$$
$$\begin{aligned}7^2&=\left(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2+\left(\sqrt{3}h\right)^2-2\left(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\left(\sqrt{3}h\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\49&=\dfrac{h^2}{3}+3h^2-h^2\\147&=7h^2\\h^2&=21\end{aligned}$$
Since $h>0$, $h=\sqrt{21}$ metres.
criteria: Substitutes into the cosine rule, or equivalent merit
Finds $CB$ and $CA$ in terms of $h$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Use the area formula with the angle at $C$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\triangle ABC}&=\dfrac{1}{2}(CB)(CA)\sin C\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\times\sqrt{3}h\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}h^2\\&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\times21\\&=\dfrac{21\sqrt{3}}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Also, with base $AB=7$ and height $w$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\triangle ABC}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times7\times w\\\dfrac{21\sqrt{3}}{4}&=\dfrac{7w}{2}\\w&=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the width of the footpath is } \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} \text{ metres}$$
criteria: Equates the area with $\dfrac{1}{2}\times7\times w$, or equivalent merit
Finds the area using $\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$, or equivalent merit

3360.stem:
An office has climate control and the temperature at any time $t$ hours is $T$ degrees Celsius, where

$$T(t)=22+3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right)\qquad t\in[0,24]$$

parts.latex: What are the minimum and maximum temperatures in this office?
can_use: Maxima and minima from the range

parts.latex:
Miss Kim brought her lunch into the office but forgot to place it in the refrigerator. The food will be spoilt if the surrounding room temperature is greater than $23.5^\circ$C for more than 3 hours.

Let $t=0$ correspond to the time which Miss Kim arrives at the office (8:00 am). What is the latest time that she should finish eating the lunch, before the food is spoilt?

solutions.latex:
Since $-1\le\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right)\le1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Minimum}&=22-3=19^\circ\text{C}\\\text{Maximum}&=22+3=25^\circ\text{C}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the minimum or the maximum, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{12}}=24$ hours.

Find when $T=23.5$:
$$\begin{aligned}23.5&=22+3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right)\\\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{\pi}{12}t=\dfrac{\pi}{6} \text{ or } \pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$
so $t=2$ or $t=10$.

The temperature is above $23.5^\circ$C from $t=2$, that is from 10 am.

$\therefore$ the latest time she should finish eating is 1 pm.

3361.stem:
Thirty Transit Officers patrolled the train line between Strathfield and Hornsby for three days. The number of ticket infringements issued by each Transit Officer over their three day blitz is summarised in the following table.

\extable{1334_q20_t1}

parts.latex: Calculate the mean number of infringements issued over the past three days. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
parts.note: Mean of a data set from a frequency table: summary statistics of data are not in 2024 Advanced (Standard).

parts.latex: Calculate the standard deviation. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
parts.note: Standard deviation of a data set is removed (Mathematics Standard).

parts.latex: Determine the median number of infringements issued and describe the skewness of the data.

There are 120 Transit Officers patrolling the rail network. Use the sample data in the table to estimate how many of these Transit Officer would have issued more than two ticketing infringements within their three day blitz.

solutions.latex: $$\bar{x}=\dfrac{(12\times0)+(5\times1)+(6\times2)+(3\times3)+(3\times4)+(1\times5)}{30}\approx1.43$$
$$\begin{aligned}\sigma&=\sqrt{\dfrac{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2f_i}{n}}\\&=1.4985\ldots\\&\approx1.50\end{aligned}$$

There are 30 values, so the median is the mean of the 15th and 16th values.
$$\text{Median}=\dfrac{1+1}{2}=1$$
The data is positively skewed.
criteria: Finds the median or describes the skewness, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$7\times4=28$$
$\therefore$ about 28 Transit Officers.

parts.latex:
The September sale prices for properties (in dollars) in a suburb sold by a particular real estate agent were:

$747\,000,\ 768\,000,\ 887\,000,\ 895\,000,\ 959\,000,$ and $986\,000$

On the 1st of October they realised they had omitted a sale price of $992\,000$.

If this sale price was included in the September summary, what effect would it have on the mean and median?

solutions.latex:
The new price $\$992\,000$ is above the existing values, so the mean increases.

The median changes to $\$895\,000$.
criteria: States the effect on the mean or on the median, or equivalent merit

3363.stem:
A computer repair store summarised the repair inquiries they received in one month in the following table:

\extable{1334_q21_t1}

figures.cap: solution sketch: Pareto chart of repair inquiries

parts.latex: Fill in the table's cumulative percentage column and construct the Pareto chart for this information.

parts.latex: Which computer problems account for $70\%$ of the inquiries? Give a reason for why this may be the case.
parts.note: Interpreting a Pareto chart is not in 2024 Advanced.

criteria: Column graph in descending order or cumulative line graph, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Screen, malfunctioning trackpad and malfunctioning key on keyboard account for about $70\%$ of inquiries (cumulative $73\%$).

These problems relate to the external components of the computer, which are prone to damage and so require more repairs.
criteria: Identifies the three problems or gives a reason, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Differentiate $\ln(\tan 3x)$.

solutions.latex: $$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\ln(\tan3x)\right)=\dfrac{3\sec^23x}{\tan3x}$$
criteria: Differentiates $\tan 3x$ or applies the log derivative rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Differentiate $\dfrac{x}{e^{3x+1}}$.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=e^{3x+1}\\u'&=1 & v'&=3e^{3x+1}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x}{e^{3x+1}}\right)&=\dfrac{e^{3x+1}(1)-x\left(3e^{3x+1}\right)}{\left(e^{3x+1}\right)^2}\\&=\dfrac{e^{3x+1}(1-3x)}{\left(e^{3x+1}\right)^2}\\&=\dfrac{1-3x}{e^{3x+1}}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=\log_e\left(2x^2+1\right)$ at the point $(2,\log_e 9)$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating, using the chain rule for $\ln$:
$$y'=\dfrac{4x}{2x^2+1}$$
At $x=2$:
$$y'=\dfrac{4(2)}{2(2^2)+1}=\dfrac{8}{9}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so
$$m_N=\dfrac{-1}{m_T}=-\dfrac{9}{8}$$
The equation of the normal is
$$y-\log_e 9=-\dfrac{9}{8}(x-2)$$
$$y=-\dfrac{9}{8}x+\log_e 9+\dfrac{9}{4}$$
The general form $9x+8y-18-8\log_e 9=0$ is also acceptable.
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit
Finds the derivative and the gradient of the tangent $\dfrac{8}{9}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find: $\displaystyle\int\left(1+e^{7x}\right)dx$

solutions.latex: $$\int\left(1+e^{7x}\right)dx=x+\dfrac{1}{7}e^{7x}+C$$
criteria: Integrates one term correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Evaluate: $\displaystyle\int_0^2\dfrac{2}{5x+4}\,dx$

solutions.latex:
Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(5x+4)=\dfrac{5}{5x+4}$, write the integrand with a factor of $5$ in the numerator.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^2\dfrac{2}{5x+4}\,dx&=\dfrac{2}{5}\int_0^2\dfrac{5}{5x+4}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{2}{5}\Big[\ln(5x+4)\Big]_0^2\\&=\dfrac{2}{5}\left(\ln 14-\ln 4\right)\\&=\dfrac{2}{5}\ln\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct primitive, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{2x}\right)$.

Hence or otherwise, find

$$\int xe^{2x}\,dx$$

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=e^{2x}\\u'&=1 & v'&=2e^{2x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{2x}\right)&=1\cdot e^{2x}+x\cdot 2e^{2x}\\&=2xe^{2x}+e^{2x}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (a), integrating both sides:
$$xe^{2x}+C=\displaystyle\int\left(2xe^{2x}+e^{2x}\right)dx$$
Rearranging:
$$2\int xe^{2x}\,dx=xe^{2x}-\int e^{2x}\,dx=xe^{2x}-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{2x}+C$$
Dividing by $2$:
$$\int xe^{2x}\,dx=\dfrac{x}{2}e^{2x}-\dfrac{1}{4}e^{2x}+\dfrac{C}{2}$$
criteria: Rearranges using part (a), or equivalent merit

figures.cap: graph of f(x)=9-3^(x+1) from A on the y-axis to B on the x-axis with chord AB, region between shaded

parts.latex:
Part of the graph of the function $f(x)=9-3^{x+1}$ is shown below.

\exfigure{1334_q26_1}

$f(x)$ intersects the axes at the points $A$ and $B$. The line joining $A$ and $B$ is also shown.

Show that the exact value of the shaded area is

$$6-\dfrac{6}{\ln 3}$$

solutions.latex:
When $x=0$:
$$f(0)=9-3=6$$
When $y=0$:
$$3^{x+1}=3^2,\quad x=1$$
So $A(0,6)$ and $B(1,0)$.

The shaded area is the area under the curve less the triangle under the line $AB$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=\int_0^1\left(9-3^{x+1}\right)dx-\dfrac{1}{2}(1\times 6)\\&=\left[9x-\dfrac{3^{x+1}}{\ln 3}\right]_0^1-3\\&=\left[\left(9-\dfrac{3^2}{\ln 3}\right)-\left(0-\dfrac{3}{\ln 3}\right)\right]-3\\&=9-\dfrac{6}{\ln 3}-3\\&=6-\dfrac{6}{\ln 3}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the area integral minus the triangle, or equivalent merit
Finds the coordinates of $A$ and $B$, or equivalent merit

3371.stem: A sports magazine surveyed 120 soccer fans and asked them whether they supported Manchester United or Tottenham. 74 fans supported Manchester United, 55 supported Tottenham and 8 supported neither team.

figures.cap: solution sketch: Venn diagram M 57, both 17, T 38, neither 8

parts.latex: Represent this data in a Venn diagram in the space below.
A fan is selected at random. If the fan selected is a Manchester United fan, what is the probability that they are also a Tottenham fan?

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw: Venn diagram with two overlapping circles inside a rectangle: M only 57, both M and T 17, T only 38, outside both 8. Source gave only the values. Sketch id given on the item is 1334_q27_s2 while the figure key in the text is 1334_q27_s1.

3372.stem: Elysia and Leo are playing a game, they take turns throwing two dice. The game is won by the first player to throw a double six. Elysia starts the game.

parts.latex: What is the probability that Elysia wins the game on the first throw.
What is the probability that Elysia wins the game on the first or on the second throw?
Find the probability that Elysia eventually wins the game.

solutions.latex:
A double six needs a six on each die.
$$P(\text{win first throw})=\dfrac{1}{6}\times\dfrac{1}{6}=\dfrac{1}{36}$$

To win on the second throw, both players miss the first time, then Elysia throws a double six.
$$P(\text{win on second throw})=\dfrac{35}{36}\times\dfrac{35}{36}\times\dfrac{1}{36}$$
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{win first or second throw})&=\dfrac{1}{36}+\dfrac{35}{36}\times\dfrac{35}{36}\times\dfrac{1}{36}\\&=\dfrac{2521}{46656}\\&\approx 0.054\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the probability of winning on the second throw, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Elysia wins on her 1st, 2nd, 3rd, ... throw, so
$$\dfrac{1}{36}+\dfrac{1}{36}\left(\dfrac{35}{36}\right)^2+\dfrac{1}{36}\left(\dfrac{35}{36}\right)^4+\cdots$$
This is a geometric series with $a=\dfrac{1}{36}$ and $r=\left(\dfrac{35}{36}\right)^2$. Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum exists.
$$\begin{aligned}S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\\&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{36}}{1-\left(\frac{35}{36}\right)^2}\\&=\dfrac{36}{71}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Identifies the geometric series with $a$ and $r$, or equivalent merit

3373.stem:
Mr Park has built a new brick wall in his backyard to patch up the hole that had been created when a car ran into his fence.

The bottom row has 75 bricks, and each of the rows 2, 3, ..., 20 has 3 fewer bricks than the row below it.

Above row 20, each row has 1 brick fewer than the row below it. The top row has 10 bricks.

\exfigure{1334_q29_1}

figures.cap: brick wall rows 1, 2, 20, 21 shown

parts.latex: How many bricks are in row 20?
What is the total number of rows in the wall?
How many bricks are used in the construction of the wall?

solutions.latex:
The rows form an arithmetic sequence with $a=75$ and $d=-3$, so
$$T_n=a+(n-1)d$$
$$\begin{aligned}T_{20}&=75+(20-1)(-3)\\&=18\end{aligned}$$
So there are $18$ bricks in row 20.

Row 20 has $18$ bricks, and each row above has one fewer.

So row 21 has $17$ bricks, and the numbers continue $16,15,\ldots$ down to the top row with $10$ bricks.

The rows above row 20 have $17,16,\ldots,10$ bricks, which is $17-10+1=8$ rows.

Total rows: $20+8=28$.

meta.format_note: Source line '$18+10=28$ rows...' was a slip in wording; replaced by a count of the 8 rows (17 down to 10), giving the same answer 28.

solutions.latex:
Rows 1 to 20 form an arithmetic series with $a=75$ and $l=18$.
$$\begin{aligned}S_{20}&=\dfrac{20}{2}(75+18)\\&=930\end{aligned}$$
Rows 21 to 28 have $17,16,\ldots,10$ bricks, an arithmetic series of $8$ terms.
$$\begin{aligned}S&=\dfrac{8}{2}(17+10)\\&=108\end{aligned}$$
Total:
$$930+108=1038 \text{ bricks}$$
criteria: Finds the sums of the two sections (930 and 108), or equivalent merit

3374.stem:
Scientists have recently discovered a new drug to control a rare medical condition. It is known that the quantity $Q$ of the drug remaining in the body after $t$ hours satisfies an equation of the form

$$Q=Q_0e^{-kt}$$

where $Q_0$ and $k$ are positive constants.

The initial dose is 5 milligrams and after 17 hours the amount remaining in the body is half the initial dose.

parts.latex: Find the exact values of $Q_0$ and $k$.
When will one-seventh of the initial dose remain?

solutions.latex:
When $t=0$, $Q=5$:
$$5=Q_0e^{-k(0)}$$
so $Q_0=5$.

When $t=17$, $Q=\dfrac{5}{2}$:
$$\dfrac{5}{2}=5e^{-17k}$$
$$\dfrac{1}{2}=e^{-17k}$$
Taking natural logarithms:
$$\begin{aligned}\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&=-17k\\k&=-\dfrac{1}{17}\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{17}\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $Q_0=5$ and sets up $\dfrac{5}{2}=5e^{-17k}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
One-seventh of the initial dose is $Q=\dfrac{5}{7}$.
$$\dfrac{5}{7}=5e^{-kt}$$
$$e^{-kt}=\dfrac{1}{7}$$
$$-kt=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{7}\right)$$
$$\begin{aligned}t&=-\dfrac{1}{k}\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{7}\right)\\&=\dfrac{17}{\ln 2}\ln 7\\&\approx 47.725\ldots\\&\approx 48 \text{ hours}\end{aligned}$$

3375.stem:
A particle with velocity, $v$ ms$^{-1}$ moves along a straight line from a fixed point $O$

$$v=-4\cos t$$

where the time $t$ is measured in seconds from $t=0$.

It is initially 1 metre to the right of the origin.

parts.latex: When, and where, does the particle first come to rest?
Show that the total distance travelled by the particle between $0\le t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ is $\left(8-2\sqrt{3}\right)$ metres.

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$-4\cos t=0,\quad \cos t=0$$
so $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2},\ldots$ and the first time is $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

The displacement is the integral of the velocity.
$$x=\int-4\cos t\,dt=-4\sin t+C$$
When $t=0$, $x=1$, so $C=1$ and
$$x=1-4\sin t$$
At $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$x=1-4=-3$$
The particle first comes to rest when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ seconds, at $3$ m to the left of the origin.

The particle changes direction at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ (where $v=0$), so split the distance there.
$$\text{Distance}=\left|\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}-4\cos t\,dt\right|+\left|\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{2\pi}{3}}-4\cos t\,dt\right|$$
$$\begin{aligned}&=\left|-4\Big[\sin t\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\right|+\left|-4\Big[\sin t\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{2\pi}{3}}\right|\\&=\left|-4(1-0)\right|+\left|-4\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-1\right)\right|\\&=4+\left(4-2\sqrt{3}\right)\\&=8-2\sqrt{3}\text{ metres}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Integrates correctly over both intervals, or equivalent merit
Splits the distance at the change of direction, or equivalent merit

3376.stem:
A ride sharing vehicle is to complete an interstate trip totalling 1000 kilometres at a constant speed of $v$ km/h. When travelling at this speed the car consumes fuel at the rate of

$$\left(6+\dfrac{v^2}{50}\right)\text{ litres per hour.}$$

As a bonus, the company has offered to pay 50 cents per litre for fuel and for safety, two drivers where they will each be paid 45 dollars per hour whilst they are completing the trip.

parts.latex:
Let $C$ represent the total cost of fuel and the drivers' wages for the trip.

Show that

$$C=10v+\dfrac{93000}{v}$$

if the company was to pay two drivers.

The vehicle needs to complete the 1000 kilometre journey within 12 hours, whilst remaining under the speed limit of $90$ km/h.

At what speed $v$ should the vehicle be driven at to minimise the cost $C$, whilst arriving at the destination within 12 hours?

solutions.latex:
Fuel costs $\$0.50$ per litre, so the fuel cost per hour is
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\left(6+\dfrac{v^2}{50}\right)\text{ dollars}$$
The two drivers' wages are $2\times 45=\$90$ per hour.

The trip of $1000$ km at $v$ km/h takes $\dfrac{1000}{v}$ hours.
$$\begin{aligned}C&=\text{fuel}+\text{wages}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(6+\dfrac{v^2}{50}\right)\times\dfrac{1000}{v}+90\left(\dfrac{1000}{v}\right)\\&=\dfrac{500}{v}\left(6+\dfrac{v^2}{50}\right)+\dfrac{90000}{v}\\&=\dfrac{3000}{v}+10v+\dfrac{90000}{v}\\&=10v+\dfrac{93000}{v}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes $C$ as fuel plus wages, or equivalent merit
Finds the hourly costs and the time $\dfrac{1000}{v}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $C=10v+93000v^{-1}$.
$$\dfrac{dC}{dv}=10-\dfrac{93000}{v^2}$$
Stationary point: $\dfrac{dC}{dv}=0$.
$$93000=10v^2,\quad v^2=9300$$
Since $v>0$, $v=10\sqrt{93}\approx 96.44$ km/h.

Nature test, using the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2C}{dv^2}=\dfrac{186000}{v^3}>0 \text{ at } v=10\sqrt{93}$$
so this is a minimum.

However, this speed exceeds the limit of $90$ km/h, so it is not allowed.

The time limit requires $\dfrac{1000}{v}\le 12$, so $v\ge\dfrac{1000}{12}\approx 83.33$ km/h.

The allowed speeds are $83.33\le v\le 90$.

For $v<10\sqrt{93}$, $\dfrac{dC}{dv}<0$, so $C$ is decreasing on the whole allowed interval.

Hence the cost is least at the largest allowed speed. At $90$ km/h the journey takes $\dfrac{1000}{90}\approx 11.11$ hours, which is within $12$ hours.
$$\therefore\ v=90\text{ km/h}$$
criteria: Finds the minimum $v=10\sqrt{93}$ and tests it, or equivalent merit
Differentiates and solves $\dfrac{dC}{dv}=0$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Removed the source's slightly misleading statement that the journey at 10√93 km/h 'takes about 10.37 hours' as a reason for rejection; rejection is by the speed limit, with the 12 hour constraint giving the lower bound. Answer unchanged.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of f(x)=x^3-3x^2-9x+18 with max (-1,23), min (3,-9), inflection (1,7)

parts.latex: For the function $f(x)=x^3-3x^2-9x+18$, find the stationary points, point(s) of inflection and determine the nature of the stationary points. Then sketch the graph of $f(x)$, showing the turning points and point(s) of inflection.

solutions.latex:
Stationary points: $f'(x)=0$.
$$f'(x)=3x^2-6x-9=3(x-3)(x+1)=0$$
so $x=-1$ or $x=3$.
$$f(-1)=(-1)^3-3(-1)^2-9(-1)+18=23$$
$$f(3)=3^3-3(3^2)-9(3)+18=-9$$
Nature, using the second derivative:
$$f''(x)=6x-6$$
$$f''(-1)=-12<0\text{, so }(-1,23)\text{ is a maximum}$$
$$f''(3)=12>0\text{, so }(3,-9)\text{ is a minimum}$$
Possible inflection: $f''(x)=6(x-1)=0$, so $x=1$ and
$$f(1)=1-3-9+18=7$$
Test the concavity either side of $x=1$:

\extable{Ts4846_1}

The concavity changes, so $(1,7)$ is a point of inflection.

\exfigure{1334_q33_s1}
criteria: Correct sketch with most features, or equivalent merit
Finds the nature of the stationary points and the point of inflection, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary points with $y$-values, or equivalent merit
Finds $f'(x)$ and the $x$-values of the stationary points, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw: graph of f(x)=x^3-3x^2-9x+18 with maximum (-1,23), minimum (3,-9), point of inflection (1,7) (concave down to concave up), y-intercept (0,18). x-intercepts: f(x)=(x-3)(x^2-9)... factor check: f(x)=(x-3)^2? not factored in source; mark x=3 stationary only. Criteria: source had 1,1,1,2 marks; rewritten top-down. Source marks sum to 5.

parts.latex: $2\log_{10}(x)-\log_{10}(3x)$ is equal to

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws, $a\log_{10}b=\log_{10}b^a$ and $\log_{10}a-\log_{10}b=\log_{10}\dfrac{a}{b}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\log_{10}(x)-\log_{10}(3x) &= \log_{10}(x^2)-\log_{10}(3x) \\ &= \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{x^2}{3x}\right) \\ &= \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right) \end{aligned}$$
This matches option A.

Since $1+x^2>0$ for all $x$, the sign of $f''(x)$ is the sign of $2x$.
$$2x>0$$

parts.latex:

$$3,6,12,24,\dots,384$$

solutions.latex:
For a geometric sequence, $T_n=ar^{n-1}$, with $a=3$ and $r=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} 384 &= 3\times 2^{n-1} \\ 128 &= 2^{n-1} \\ 2^7 &= 2^{n-1} \\ n &= 8 \end{aligned}$$
There are 8 terms, which is option B.

parts.latex: The solution to the inequality $6-x-x^2\le0$ is

solutions.latex:
Factorise:
$$6-x-x^2=(3+x)(2-x)\le 0$$
The parabola is concave down with roots $x=-3$ and $x=2$.

So it is below or on the axis outside the roots.
$$\therefore\ x\le -3 \text{ or } x\ge 2$$
This is option A.

parts.latex:
If $P(A)=0.8$, $P(B)=0.5$ and $P(B|A)=0.4$,

What is the value of $P(A\cap B)$?

solutions.latex:
Using the conditional probability formula:
$$P(B|A)=\dfrac{P(B\cap A)}{P(A)}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 0.4 &= \dfrac{P(B\cap A)}{0.8} \\ P(B\cap A) &= 0.4\times 0.8 \\ &= 0.32 \end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

parts.latex: If $A$ and $B$ are two independent events, then the probability of occurrence of at least one of $A$ and $B$ is given by:

solutions.latex:
"At least one of $A$ and $B$" is the event $A\cup B$.

For independent events, $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cup B) &= P(A)+P(B)-P(A)P(B) \\ &= P(A)+P(B)\left(1-P(A)\right) \\ &= P(A)+P(B)P(\bar{A}) \\ &= 1-P(\bar{A})+P(B)P(\bar{A}) \\ &= 1-P(\bar{A})\left[1-P(B)\right] \\ &= 1-P(\bar{A})P(\bar{B}) \end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

3390.stem: Differentiate the following with respect to $x$:

parts.latex: $y=\dfrac{\log_e x}{6x}$
$y=e^{2x}\sin x$

solutions.latex:
Write the function as a power and use the chain rule.
$$y=(4-x^2)^{\frac12}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac12(4-x^2)^{-\frac12}\cdot(-2x) \\ &= -\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{4-x^2}} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the chain rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\log_e x & v&=6x\\ u'&=\dfrac1x & v'&=6\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{6x\cdot\frac1x-\log_e x\cdot 6}{(6x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{6-6\log_e x}{36x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{1-\log_e x}{6x^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{2x} & v&=\sin x\\ u'&=2e^{2x} & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= e^{2x}\cos x+\sin x\cdot 2e^{2x} \\ &= e^{2x}(\cos x+2\sin x) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:

$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int\dfrac{x+2}{x^2+4x-6}\,dx &= \dfrac12\displaystyle\int\dfrac{2x+4}{x^2+4x-6}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac12\log_e|x^2+4x-6|+C \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_0^2 3^{-x}\,dx &= \left[\dfrac{3^{-x}}{\ln\left(\frac13\right)}\right]_0^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\log_e 3}\left(1-\dfrac19\right) \\ &= \dfrac{8}{9\log_e 3} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Show that $\cot A+\dfrac{\sin A}{1+\cos A}=\operatorname{cosec}A$

solutions.latex:
Start with the left-hand side and write $\cot A=\dfrac{\cos A}{\sin A}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\cos A}{\sin A}+\dfrac{\sin A}{1+\cos A} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos A+\cos^2A+\sin^2A}{\sin A(1+\cos A)} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos A+1}{\sin A(1+\cos A)} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sin A} \\ &= \operatorname{cosec}A \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Combines into a single fraction, or equivalent merit

3398.stem:
A yacht is located at point $Y$ and is sailing on a bearing of $032^\circ T$ towards a lighthouse at point $L$ 1.5 km from point $Y$. From $Y$, the yacht’s navigator spots a boat at point $B$ bearing $120^\circ T$. The bearing of the lighthouse from the boat is $332^\circ T$.

\exfigure{1335_q19_1}

figures.cap: bearings diagram of yacht Y, lighthouse L and boat B, not to scale

parts.latex: Calculate the distance between the yacht and the boat.

parts.latex: From the boat, the top of the lighthouse has an elevation of $2^\circ$. Determine the height of the lighthouse above sea level.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: angle of elevation of the lighthouse top from a boat, using a horizontal bearings triangle (now Year 11 Extension 1)

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1335_q19_s1}

The bearings of $L$ and $B$ from $Y$ are $032^\circ$ and $120^\circ$.

$$\angle LYB=120^\circ-32^\circ=88^\circ$$

From $B$, $L$ is at $332^\circ$ and $Y$ is at $300^\circ$ (the reverse of $120^\circ$).

$$\angle LBY=360^\circ-332^\circ+(300^\circ-300^\circ)=32^\circ$$

Angle sum in $\triangle LYB$:

$$\angle YLB=180^\circ-88^\circ-32^\circ=60^\circ$$

Using the sine rule in $\triangle LYB$:

$$\dfrac{YB}{\sin60^\circ}=\dfrac{1.5}{\sin32^\circ}$$

$$\begin{aligned} YB&=\dfrac{1.5\sin60^\circ}{\sin32^\circ}\\ &\approx 2.45 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the angles in the triangle and sets up the sine rule, or equivalent merit
Finds one relevant angle, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Solve the following equation for $x$

$$5^x-\dfrac{8}{5^x}=2$$

solutions.latex:
Let $m=5^x$, so the equation becomes

$$m-\dfrac{8}{m}=2$$

Multiply by $m$:

$$\begin{aligned} m^2-8&=2m\\ m^2-2m-8&=0\\ (m-4)(m+2)&=0 \end{aligned}$$

So $m=4$ or $m=-2$, that is $5^x=4$ or $5^x=-2$.

$5^x>0$ for all $x$, so $5^x=-2$ has no solution.

$$\begin{aligned} x&=\log_5 4\\ &=\dfrac{\ln4}{\ln5}\\ &\approx 0.86 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Solves the quadratic in $m$ and rejects $m=-2$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the $x$ coordinate(s) of the stationary point(s) on the curve $y=3\log_e x+x^2-7x$, where $x>0$.
Hence, determine the nature of each of the stationary point(s)

solutions.latex:
Differentiating:

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3}{x}+2x-7$$

Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3}{x}+2x-7&=0\\ 2x^2-7x+3&=0 &&(\text{multiply by } x)\\ (2x-1)(x-3)&=0 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{1}{2} \text{ or } x=3$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating again:

$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-\dfrac{3}{x^2}+2$$

At $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$:

$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-3\times4+2=-10<0$$

so there is a maximum turning point at $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

At $x=3$:

$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-\dfrac{3}{9}+2=\dfrac{5}{3}>0$$

so there is a minimum turning point at $x=3$.
criteria: Finds $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ and correctly tests one stationary point, or equivalent merit

3403.stem: There are some red counters and some white counters in a bag. At the start, 7 of the counters are red and the rest of the counters are white. Woody takes two counters from the bag. First he takes at random a counter from the bag. He does not put the counter back in the bag. Woody then takes at random another counter from the bag.

figures.cap: solution sketch: worked tree diagram for counters

parts.latex:
Let the number of white counters in the bag be $x$.

Draw a tree diagram that represents the above scenario, showing all relevant information.

It is given that the probability that the first counter Woody takes is white, and the second counter Woody takes is red is $\dfrac{21}{80}$.

Find the number of white counters in the bag at the start.

criteria: Draws a tree diagram with some correct probabilities, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Tree diagram figure kept as in the source (id 1335_q24_s1; the sketch_id given is 1335_q24_s2, check which exists). Expected tree: first draw $W$ with $\dfrac{x}{x+7}$, $R$ with $\dfrac{7}{x+7}$; after $W$: $W$ $\dfrac{x-1}{x+6}$, $R$ $\dfrac{7}{x+6}$; after $R$: $W$ $\dfrac{x}{x+6}$, $R$ $\dfrac{6}{x+6}$. Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
From the tree diagram, $P(WR)=\dfrac{x}{x+7}\times\dfrac{7}{x+6}$.

$$\dfrac{x}{x+7}\times\dfrac{7}{x+6}=\dfrac{21}{80}$$

Divide both sides by $7$:

$$\dfrac{x}{(x+7)(x+6)}=\dfrac{3}{80}$$

$$\begin{aligned} 80x&=3(x+7)(x+6)\\ &=3(x^2+13x+42)\\ &=3x^2+39x+126 \end{aligned}$$

$$3x^2-41x+126=0$$

$$\begin{aligned} x&=\dfrac{41\pm\sqrt{169}}{6}\\ &=\dfrac{41\pm13}{6}\\ &=9 \text{ or } 4\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$

$x$ is a whole number of counters, so $x=9$.

$$\therefore\ \text{there are 9 white counters.}$$
criteria: Forms the equation $\dfrac{x}{x+7}\times\dfrac{7}{x+6}=\dfrac{21}{80}$, or equivalent merit

3404.stem: A geometric sequence is such that its sum of the first 4 terms is 17 times its sum of the first 2 terms. It is given that the common ratio of this geometric sequence is positive and not equal to 1.

parts.latex: Find the common ratio of this geometric sequence.
Given that the $6^{\text{th}}$ term of this geometric sequence is 64. Find the first term.
Does this sequence have a limiting sum? Explain your reasoning.

solutions.latex:
For a geometric sequence, $S_4=\dfrac{a(r^4-1)}{r-1}$ and $S_2=a+ar=a(1+r)$.

Given $S_4=17S_2$:

$$\dfrac{a(r^4-1)}{r-1}=17a(1+r)$$

Dividing by $a\ne0$ and multiplying by $r-1$:

$$r^4-1=17(r^2-1)$$

$$\begin{aligned} (r^2-1)(r^2+1)&=17(r^2-1)\\ (r^2-1)(r^2+1-17)&=0\\ (r^2-1)(r^2-16)&=0 \end{aligned}$$

So $r=\pm1$ or $r=\pm4$.

The ratio is positive and $r\ne1$, so $r=4$.
criteria: Forms and factorises the equation in $r$, or equivalent merit
Writes $S_4$ and $S_2$ and forms an equation in $r$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The $n$th term is $T_n=ar^{n-1}$, so $T_6=ar^5$.

$$\begin{aligned} 64&=a(4)^5\\ a&=\dfrac{64}{4^5}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{16} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
A limiting sum exists only when $-1<r<1$.

Here $r=4$, which is not in this range.

$$\therefore\ \text{the sequence does not have a limiting sum.}$$

parts.latex: Determine the number of solutions for $\sin\theta=-0.7$, where $\theta\in[0,51\pi]$ and provide reasons for your answer.

solutions.latex:
The period of $\sin\theta$ is $2\pi$, and $\sin\theta=-0.7$ has two solutions in each period.

For $\theta\in[0,50\pi]$ there are $25$ periods, giving $25\times2=50$ solutions.

For $\theta\in[50\pi,51\pi]$, which is the first half of a period, $\sin\theta\ge0$, so there are no solutions.

$$\therefore\ \text{there are 50 solutions.}$$
criteria: Finds the solutions in $[0,50\pi]$ and considers $[50\pi,51\pi]$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The Richter scale defines the magnitude of an earthquake as $M=\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{I}{S}\right)$ where $I$ is the intensity of the earthquake wave, and $S$ is the intensity of the smallest detectable wave.

An earthquake that registered 6.4 in magnitude was followed by another which was 4 times more intense.

Determine the magnitude of the second earthquake accurate to 1 decimal place.

solutions.latex:
For the first earthquake:

$$6.4=\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{I_1}{S}\right)\text{, so } \dfrac{I_1}{S}=10^{6.4}$$

The second earthquake has $I_2=4I_1$.

$$\begin{aligned} M_2&=\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{I_2}{S}\right)\\ &=\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{4I_1}{S}\right)\\ &=\log_{10}\left(4\times10^{6.4}\right)\\ &=\log_{10}4+6.4\\ &\approx 7.0 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the magnitude is } 7.0 \text{ (to 1 decimal place).}$$

figures.cap: two circles, shaded crescent region right of chord CD

solutions.latex:
In right-angled $\triangle ABC$ (right angle at $A$), $AB=AC=r$, so by Pythagoras:

$$BC=\sqrt{2}\,r$$

Since $AB=AC$, $\angle ABC=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, so $\angle CBD=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Using the segment formula $\dfrac{1}{2}R^2(\theta-\sin\theta)$ with $R=\sqrt{2}\,r$ and $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area of segment } CD&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{2}\,r\right)^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\\ &=r^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-1\right) \end{aligned}$$

The shaded region is the semicircle on diameter $CD$ (radius $r$) less this segment:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Shaded area}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\pi r^2-\left(\dfrac{\pi r^2}{2}-r^2\right)\\ &=r^2 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the area of the segment, or equivalent merit
Finds $BC$ or $\angle CBD$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Show that the area of the isosceles triangle can be expressed as

$$A=12+9\tan\theta+4\cot\theta$$
Hence, find the minimum area of the isosceles triangle that inscribes the rectangle.

solutions.latex:
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$, $FM=y$, and $CE=x$.

The area of the triangle is

$$A=\dfrac{1}{2}bh\text{, with } b=2x+6 \text{ and } h=y+2$$

In the small right-angled triangle at $E$ (opposite side $2$, adjacent side $x$):

$$\tan\theta=\dfrac{2}{x}\text{, so } x=2\cot\theta$$

In the right-angled triangle with $FM=y$ and half the width $3$ (angle $\theta$ at the base, by the isosceles triangle and parallel lines):

$$\tan\theta=\dfrac{y}{3}\text{, so } y=3\tan\theta$$

$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{1}{2}(2x+6)(y+2)\\ &=(x+3)(y+2)\\ &=xy+2x+3y+6\\ &=6+2(2\cot\theta)+3(3\tan\theta)+6\\ &=12+4\cot\theta+9\tan\theta \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $x$ and $y$ in terms of $\theta$ and substitutes into the area, or equivalent merit
Finds $x$ or $y$ in terms of $\theta$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Write $A=12+4(\tan\theta)^{-1}+9\tan\theta$ and differentiate:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{d\theta}&=-4(\tan\theta)^{-2}\sec^2\theta+9\sec^2\theta\\ &=-\dfrac{4}{\sin^2\theta}+\dfrac{9}{\cos^2\theta}\\ &=\dfrac{-4\cos^2\theta+9\sin^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta} \end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} 9\sin^2\theta&=4\cos^2\theta\\ \tan^2\theta&=\dfrac{4}{9}\\ \tan\theta&=\dfrac{2}{3} &&(0<\theta<90^\circ) \end{aligned}$$

so $\theta\approx33^\circ41'$.

Test the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}$ either side:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{d\theta}&=-4 &&\text{at } 30^\circ\\ \dfrac{dA}{d\theta}&=0 &&\text{at } 33^\circ41'\\ \dfrac{dA}{d\theta}&=10 &&\text{at } 45^\circ \end{aligned}$$

The gradient changes from negative to positive, so this is a minimum.

When $\tan\theta=\dfrac{2}{3}$, $\cot\theta=\dfrac{3}{2}$:

$$\begin{aligned} A&=12+4\cdot\dfrac{3}{2}+9\cdot\dfrac{2}{3}\\ &=24 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum area is } 24 \text{ cm}^2$$
criteria: Finds $\tan\theta=\dfrac{2}{3}$ and tests that it is a minimum, or equivalent merit
Finds $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}$ and sets it to zero, or equivalent merit
Attempts to differentiate $A$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The first four numbers of an arithmetic sequence are $p, 9, 3p-q, 3p+q$.

Find the 2022th term.

solutions.latex:
The common difference is $d=(3p+q)-(3p-q)=2q$.

Using the first two terms:

$$9-p=2q\text{, so } p+2q=9 \quad (1)$$

Using the second and third terms:

$$9+2q=3p-q\text{, so } 3p-3q=9\text{, i.e. } p-q=3 \quad (2)$$

Subtract (2) from (1):

$$3q=6\text{, so } q=2 \text{ and } p=5$$

The sequence is $5,\ 9,\ 13,\ 17,\dots$ with $a=5$ and $d=4$.

$$\begin{aligned} T_{2022}&=a+2021d\\ &=5+2021\times4\\ &=8089 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Forms two equations in $p$ and $q$, or equivalent merit
Finds the common difference in terms of $q$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Given that $y=xe^{-x}$, find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ and hence show that

$$\int xe^{-x}\,dx=-xe^{-x}-e^{-x}+C$$

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=e^{-x}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x\cdot(-e^{-x})+e^{-x}=-xe^{-x}+e^{-x}$$

Integrating both sides:

$$\int(-xe^{-x}+e^{-x})\,dx=xe^{-x}+C_1$$

$$-\int xe^{-x}\,dx+\int e^{-x}\,dx=xe^{-x}+C_1$$

$$\begin{aligned} \int xe^{-x}\,dx&=-xe^{-x}+\int e^{-x}\,dx\\ &=-xe^{-x}-e^{-x}+C \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ and integrates it, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
From (a), $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^{-x}(1-x)$.

At $x=2$ the gradient of the tangent is $m_T=-\dfrac{1}{e^2}$.

$$\begin{aligned} y-\dfrac{2}{e^2}&=-\dfrac{1}{e^2}(x-2)\\ y&=-\dfrac{1}{e^2}x+\dfrac{4}{e^2} \end{aligned}$$

The tangent is above the curve between $x=0$ and $x=2$, so the area is

$$\int_0^2\left(-\dfrac{1}{e^2}x+\dfrac{4}{e^2}-xe^{-x}\right)dx$$

Using the result of part (a):

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\left[-\dfrac{1}{2e^2}x^2+\dfrac{4}{e^2}x+xe^{-x}+e^{-x}\right]_0^2\\ &=\left(-\dfrac{2}{e^2}+\dfrac{8}{e^2}+\dfrac{2}{e^2}+\dfrac{1}{e^2}\right)-(0+0+0+1)\\ &=\dfrac{9}{e^2}-1 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Given that $E(aX+b)=aE(X)+b$, where $E(X)$ is the expected value of a discrete random variable $X$ and $a$ and $b$ are constants.

Prove that $Var(aX+b)=a^2\,Var(X)$

solutions.latex:
Using $Var(X)=E(X^2)-\left[E(X)\right]^2$ for the variable $aX+b$:

$$\begin{aligned} Var(aX+b)&=E\left((aX+b)^2\right)-\left[E(aX+b)\right]^2\\ &=E(a^2X^2+2abX+b^2)-\left[aE(X)+b\right]^2\\ &=a^2E(X^2)+2abE(X)+b^2-a^2\left(E(X)\right)^2-2abE(X)-b^2\\ &=a^2\left(E(X^2)-\left(E(X)\right)^2\right)\\ &=a^2\,Var(X) \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: At the point $(2,-5)$ on the curve $y=f(x)$, the tangent has the equation $2x-y-9=0$. Determine the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=4-2f\left(3+\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$ at the point $(-2,14)$, showing all reasoning.

solutions.latex:
The tangent is transformed in the same way as the curve.

$y=4-2f\left(3+\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$ gives

$$-\dfrac{y-4}{2}=f\left(3+\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$$

In $2x-y-9=0$, replace $y$ with $-\dfrac{y-4}{2}$ and $x$ with $3+\dfrac{x}{2}$:

$$\begin{aligned} 2\left(3+\dfrac{x}{2}\right)-\left(\dfrac{4-y}{2}\right)-9&=0\\ 12+2x-(4-y)-18&=0 &&(\text{multiply by } 2)\\ 2x+y-10&=0\\ y&=-2x+10 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ y=-2x+10$$
criteria: Substitutes the transformation into the tangent equation, or equivalent merit
Identifies the transformation of $x$ or $y$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which of the following graphs best represents $y=x^2+2x-3$ ?

solutions.latex:
Factorise to find the $x$-intercepts.
$$y=x^2+2x-3=(x+3)(x-1)$$
So the $x$-intercepts are $x=-3$ and $x=1$, and the $y$-intercept is $-3$.

The coefficient of $x^2$ is positive, so the parabola is concave up.

The axis of symmetry is halfway between the intercepts, $x=\dfrac{-3+1}{2}=-1$, so the vertex $(-1,-4)$ lies to the left of the $y$-axis.

Only graph B is concave up, cuts the $y$-axis below the origin, and has its vertex to the left of the $y$-axis with the roots on either side of it. Graph C has its vertex on the right, and A and D are concave down.

parts.latex:
Two standard unbiased dice (with faces numbered 1 to 6) are rolled.

What is the probability of rolling at least one six?
can_use: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

solutions.latex:
Use the complement: $P(\text{at least one six})=1-P(\text{no six})$.

For each die, $P(\text{not a six})=\dfrac{5}{6}$, and the rolls are independent.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one six}) &= 1-\dfrac{5}{6}\times\dfrac{5}{6} \\ &= 1-\dfrac{25}{36} \\ &= \dfrac{11}{36} \end{aligned}$$
This matches option B.

The curve is concave down where $f''(x)<0$.

Solve $f''(x)<0$:

parts.latex:
A function is defined by $y=\sin^2\sqrt{x-2}$.

Which of the following gives the domain and range of this function?

solutions.latex:
Domain: the square root $\sqrt{x-2}$ needs $x-2\ge 0$, so $x\ge 2$.

Range: for $x\ge 2$, $\sqrt{x-2}$ takes every value $\ge 0$, so $\sin\sqrt{x-2}$ takes every value in $[-1,1]$.

Squaring gives
$$0\le \sin^2\sqrt{x-2}\le 1.$$
So the domain is $x\ge 2$ and the range is $0\le y\le 1$, which is option D.

parts.latex:
The only stationary point on the graph $y=f(x)$ is the point $(a,b)$.

What are the coordinates of the only stationary point on the graph $y=-f(2x)$ ?

solutions.latex:
Replacing $x$ by $2x$ in $f(x)$ compresses the graph horizontally by a factor of $2$, so the $x$-coordinate $a$ becomes $\dfrac{a}{2}$.

The negative sign reflects the graph in the $x$-axis, so the $y$-coordinate $b$ becomes $-b$.

The stationary point is $\left(\dfrac{1}{2}a,-b\right)$.

Check: if $g(x)=-f(2x)$, then $g'(x)=-2f'(2x)$, which is zero when $2x=a$, so $x=\dfrac{a}{2}$, and $g\left(\dfrac{a}{2}\right)=-f(a)=-b$. This is option A.

solutions.latex:

The area between the curves is therefore
$$A=\displaystyle\int_0^a \left(g(x)-f(x)\right)dx+\int_a^b \left(f(x)-g(x)\right)dx.$$
This is option D, which is correct. It equals $\displaystyle\int_0^b |f(x)-g(x)|\,dx$, so A is correct.

On each interval one function is above the axis and the other below, so $|f-g|=|f|+|g|$. Hence C is also correct.

Option B gives $\displaystyle\int_0^b \left(|f(x)|-|g(x)|\right)dx$. This is a difference of areas, not their sum, so it is not the shaded area.

The expression that is NOT correct is option B.

solutions.latex:

parts.latex: Find simplified expressions for $f(g(x))$ and $g(f(x))$.
Show that $f(g(x))+g(f(x))=0$ has no real roots.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $g(x)$ into $f$, and $f(x)$ into $g$.
$$\begin{aligned}f(g(x))&=(x+4)^2+3\\ &=x^2+8x+19\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}g(f(x))&=(x^2+3)+4\\ &=x^2+7\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds one expression correctly, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}f(g(x))+g(f(x))&=x^2+8x+19+x^2+7\\ &=2x^2+8x+26\end{aligned}$$
For no real roots, the discriminant must be negative.
$$\begin{aligned}\Delta&=8^2-4\times 2\times 26\\ &=-144\\ &<0\end{aligned}$$
Therefore the equation has no real roots.

parts.latex:
Differentiate $f(x)=3-x^2$ from first principles.

You may use $f'(x)=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$.

solutions.latex:
Using the first principles definition:

$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\\&=\lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{\left(3-(x+h)^2\right)-\left(3-x^2\right)}{h}\\&=\lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{\left(3-x^2-2xh-h^2\right)-\left(3-x^2\right)}{h}\\&=\lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{-2xh-h^2}{h}\\&=\lim_{h\to 0}\left(-2x-h\right)\\&=-2x\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ f'(x)=-2x$$
criteria: Substitutes into the first principles formula and expands correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that the values of $b$ and $c$ are 0.4 and 0.2 respectively.
Calculate the variance for this probability distribution.

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to 1:

$$0.3+b+0.1+c=1$$

$$b+c=0.6\quad\text{so}\quad 10b+10c=6\qquad(1)$$

Using $E(X)=\displaystyle\sum x_iP(X=x_i)$:

$$4.8=2\times 0.3+4b+6\times 0.1+10c$$

$$4b+10c=3.6\qquad(2)$$

Subtracting (2) from (1):

$$\begin{aligned}6b&=2.4\\b&=0.4\end{aligned}$$

Then $c=0.6-0.4=0.2$.

$$\therefore\ b=0.4\text{ and }c=0.2$$
criteria: Forms one correct equation in $b$ and $c$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none). Part (b) of this question is a separate solution.

solutions.latex:
Using $E\left[X^2\right]=\displaystyle\sum x_i^2P(X=x_i)$ with $b=0.4$ and $c=0.2$:

$$E\left[X^2\right]=2^2\times 0.3+4^2\times 0.4+6^2\times 0.1+10^2\times 0.2=31.2$$

Using $\operatorname{Var}[X]=E\left[X^2\right]-\left(E[X]\right)^2$:

$$\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Var}[X]&=31.2-4.8^2\\&=8.16\end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of y=3(x-1)^4-4(x-1)^3+2 with stationary points and inflection points

parts.latex: Find the coordinates of any stationary points on the curve and determine their nature.
Find the coordinates of any points of inflection on the curve.
Hence, or otherwise, sketch the graph of $y=3(x-1)^4-4(x-1)^3+2$, showing the coordinates of the stationary points and points of inflection.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating:

$$y'=12x^3-12x^2=12x^2(x-1)$$

$$y''=36x^2-24x$$

For stationary points, $y'=0$, so $x=0$ or $x=1$.

When $x=0$, $y=2$. When $x=1$, $y=3-4+2=1$.

At $x=1$: $y''(1)=12>0$, so there is a minimum at $(1,1)$.

At $x=0$: $y''(0)=0$, so the second derivative test is inconclusive. Since $12x^2\ge 0$ and $x-1<0$ near $x=0$, $y'$ is negative on both sides of $x=0$, so the curve does not change direction.

Hence $(0,2)$ is a horizontal point of inflection.

$$\therefore\ \text{minimum at }(1,1),\ \text{horizontal point of inflection at }(0,2)$$
criteria: Finds both stationary points and determines the nature of one, or equivalent merit
Finds $y'$ and solves $y'=0$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Source stated a horizontal inflection from $y''(0)=0$ alone; added the one-line sign check of $y'$ either side of $x=0$ so the conclusion follows a test.

solutions.latex:
For points of inflection, $y''=0$:

$$\begin{aligned}36x^2-24x&=0\\12x(3x-2)&=0\end{aligned}$$

so $x=0$ or $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$.

Test the concavity either side of each value:

\extable{Ts4919_1}

The concavity changes at both values.

When $x=0$, $y=2$. When $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$, $y=\dfrac{38}{27}$.

$$\therefore\ \text{points of inflection at }(0,2)\text{ and }\left(\dfrac{2}{3},\dfrac{38}{27}\right)$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

The graph of $y=3(x-1)^4-4(x-1)^3+2$ is the graph of $y=3x^4-4x^3+2$ shifted right 1 unit.

So each feature from parts (a) and (b) moves right 1 unit:

$$\begin{aligned}(0,2)&\ \text{becomes}\ (1,2)\ \text{(horizontal point of inflection)}\\(1,1)&\ \text{becomes}\ (2,1)\ \text{(minimum)}\\\left(\dfrac{2}{3},\dfrac{38}{27}\right)&\ \text{becomes}\ \left(\dfrac{5}{3},\dfrac{38}{27}\right)\ \text{(point of inflection)}\end{aligned}$$

3440.stem:
The velocity-time graph of a particle moving in a straight line is shown below.

\exfigure{1336_q28_1}

figures.cap: velocity-time graph: straight line from (0,10) through (5,0)

parts.latex: Describe the motion of the particle in the first 8 seconds of the motion.
Find the acceleration of the particle.
Find the total distance travelled by the particle in the first 8 seconds.
If initially the particle is two units to the left of the origin, what is the location of the particle after 8 seconds?

solutions.latex:
The velocity is positive for the first 5 seconds and decreasing, so the particle moves in the positive direction with decreasing speed.

At 5 seconds the velocity is zero, so the particle comes to a stop, then reverses direction with increasing speed.

The velocity graph is a straight line with negative gradient, so the particle has constant acceleration in the negative direction throughout.
criteria: Describes part of the motion correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Acceleration is the gradient of the velocity-time graph.

$$\begin{aligned}a&=\dfrac{-10}{5}\\&=-2\text{ ms}^{-2}\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Distance is the total area between the graph and the $t$-axis, counting areas below the axis as positive.

For $0\le t\le 5$ the area is a triangle with base 5 and height 10. For $5\le t\le 8$ it is a triangle with base 3 and height 6.

$$\begin{aligned}\text{distance}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 10\times 5+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 3\times 6\\&=25+9\\&=34\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds one of the two areas, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the signed area: the first triangle is above the axis (positive) and the second is below (negative).

The particle starts 2 units to the left of the origin.

$$\begin{aligned}\text{position}&=-2+25-9\\&=14\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

The particle is 14 m to the right of the origin.

parts.latex:
Solve the equation $\tan^2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)+\left(\sqrt{3}+1\right)\tan\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=-\sqrt{3}$, where $0\leq x\leq\pi$.

Give answers in exact form.

solutions.latex:
Rearranging and factorising as a quadratic in $\tan\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$:

$$\begin{aligned}\tan^2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)+\left(\sqrt{3}+1\right)\tan\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)+\sqrt{3}&=0\\\left(\tan\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)+\sqrt{3}\right)\left(\tan\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)+1\right)&=0\end{aligned}$$

So $\tan\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=-\sqrt{3}$ or $\tan\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=-1$.

Since $0\le x\le\pi$, we need $-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\le x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\le\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$.

In this range:

$$x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\quad\text{or}\quad x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$$

$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\ \text{ or }\ x=\dfrac{11\pi}{12}$$
criteria: Finds both values of $x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ in the required range, or equivalent merit
Factorises the quadratic in $\tan\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$, or equivalent merit
