parts.latex:
Brendan and Michelle are taking turns in an eating competition.

In the first round, Brendan eats one M&M, with a volume of $0.5\text{ cm}^3$, or half a millilitre, and Michelle then follows by eating two M&Ms.

In the second round, Brendan eats three M&Ms and then Michelle eats four.

If they continue in this manner, how many M&Ms will Brendan eat in the final round before he runs out of room in his stomach, if it can hold 3 Litres?

solutions.latex:
Brendan eats $1,3,5,\dots$, an arithmetic sequence with $a=1$ and $d=2$.

$$T_n=1+2(n-1)$$

The stomach holds $3\text{ L}=3000\text{ cm}^3$ and each M&M is $0.5\text{ cm}^3$, so the most he can eat in total is

$$3000\div 0.5=6000\text{ M\&Ms}$$

Total eaten after $n$ rounds, using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)$:

$$\begin{aligned}S_n&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2\times 1+2(n-1)\right)\\&=n^2\end{aligned}$$

Setting $n^2=6000$ gives $n=\sqrt{6000}\approx 77.45$ $(n>0)$.

So Brendan completes 77 rounds, as he cannot fit the next round.

$$T_{77}=1+2(77-1)=153$$

$$\therefore\ \text{Brendan eats 153 M\&Ms in the final round.}$$
criteria: Finds the number of rounds, or equivalent merit
Forms $S_n=n^2$ and equates to the maximum number of M&Ms, or equivalent merit
Identifies the arithmetic sequence, or finds the maximum number of M&Ms, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none). The source's stomach limit counts only Brendan's M&Ms; kept as in source.

3443.stem:
A bag contains 2 white and 5 yellow tokens.

In a group of people, each person draws a token randomly from the bag, with replacement.

If the token is white, they answer the question “Are you a smoker?”

If a yellow token is drawn, they answer the question “Are you a non-smoker?”

They then answer either “Yes” or “No”, depending on whether they smoke or not.

Let $p$ be the probability that a randomly selected person is a smoker.

parts.latex:
Show that the probability that a randomly selected person answered “Yes” is given by:

$$P(\text{Yes})=\dfrac{5-3p}{7}.$$
It is now known that the group has 91 people and 50 of them answered “Yes”.
Find $p$.
Given a person answered “No”, find the probability that they are a non-smoker.

solutions.latex:
A white token (probability $\dfrac{2}{7}$) gives the question "Are you a smoker?", so the answer is "Yes" with probability $p$.

A yellow token (probability $\dfrac{5}{7}$) gives the question "Are you a non-smoker?", so the answer is "Yes" with probability $1-p$.

Adding the two ways of answering "Yes":

$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{Yes})&=P(W\cap\text{Yes})+P(Y\cap\text{Yes})\\&=\dfrac{2}{7}\times p+\dfrac{5}{7}\times(1-p)\\&=\dfrac{2p+5-5p}{7}\\&=\dfrac{5-3p}{7}\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. The source's tree diagram was only described in words, so it is replaced by the equivalent reasoning (no drawing required).

solutions.latex:
Using the result of part (a) with $P(\text{Yes})=\dfrac{50}{91}$:

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{50}{91}&=\dfrac{5-3p}{7}\\5-3p&=\dfrac{50}{13}\\3p&=\dfrac{15}{13}\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ p=\dfrac{5}{13}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
A non-smoker answers "No" only after drawing a white token, since the question is then "Are you a smoker?". Here $P(\text{non-smoker})=1-\dfrac{5}{13}=\dfrac{8}{13}$.

$$P(\text{No})=1-\dfrac{50}{91}=\dfrac{41}{91}$$

Using conditional probability:

$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{non-smoker}\mid\text{No})&=\dfrac{P(\text{non-smoker}\cap\text{No})}{P(\text{No})}\\&=\dfrac{\frac{8}{13}\times\frac{2}{7}}{\frac{41}{91}}\\&=\dfrac{16}{41}\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

3444.stem:
The diagram shows the graph of $y=x^{\frac{3}{2}}-3x$, which meets the $x$-axis at the origin and at the point $A(9,0)$. Tangents drawn to the curve at $O$ and $A$ meet at the point $B$.

\exfigure{1336_q32_1}

figures.cap: graph of y=x^(3/2)-3x with tangents at O and A meeting at B, shaded region

parts.latex: Show the coordinates of $B$ are $(3,-9)$.
Hence find the area of the shaded region bounded by the two lines and the curve.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $y=x^{\frac{3}{2}}-3x$:

$$y'=\dfrac{3}{2}x^{\frac{1}{2}}-3$$

Tangent at $O$: when $x=0$, $y'=-3$, so

$$y=-3x\qquad(1)$$

Tangent at $A$: when $x=9$, $y'=\dfrac{9}{2}-3=\dfrac{3}{2}$, so

$$\begin{aligned}y-0&=\dfrac{3}{2}(x-9)\\y&=\dfrac{3}{2}x-\dfrac{27}{2}\end{aligned}$$

The tangents meet where the $y$ values are equal:

$$\begin{aligned}-3x&=\dfrac{3}{2}x-\dfrac{27}{2}\\-6x&=3x-27\\9x&=27\\x&=3\end{aligned}$$

Substituting into (1): $y=-9$.

$$\therefore\ B=(3,-9)$$
criteria: Finds the equations of both tangents, or equivalent merit
Finds the gradient of one tangent, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
The shaded region is the triangle $OAB$ less the area between the curve and the $x$-axis.

The triangle has base $OA=9$ and height 9 (the $y$ value of $B$ is $-9$):

$$A_{\text{triangle}}=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 9\times 9=\dfrac{81}{2}$$

The curve is below the $x$-axis between $0$ and $9$, so take the absolute value of the integral:

$$\begin{aligned}A_{\text{curve}}&=\left|\int_0^9\left(x^{\frac{3}{2}}-3x\right)dx\right|\\&=\left|\left[\dfrac{2}{5}x^{\frac{5}{2}}-\dfrac{3}{2}x^2\right]_0^9\right|\\&=\left|\dfrac{2}{5}\times 9^{\frac{5}{2}}-\dfrac{3}{2}\times 9^2-0\right|\\&=24.3\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}A_{\text{shaded}}&=\dfrac{81}{2}-24.3\\&=16.2\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the area under the curve and the area of the triangle, or equivalent merit
Finds the area of the triangle or integrates the curve correctly, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: rectangle PQRS inscribed under y=e^(-x^2)

solutions.latex:
The curve $y=e^{-x^2}$ is even, so $P$ and $S$ are at $x=-m$ and $x=m$, and $PQ=e^{-m^2}$.

$$A=2\times OP\times PQ=2me^{-m^2}$$

For a maximum, $\dfrac{dA}{dm}=0$. Using the product rule:

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dA}{dm}&=2e^{-m^2}+2me^{-m^2}(-2m)\\&=2e^{-m^2}\left(1-2m^2\right)\\&=0\end{aligned}$$

Since $e^{-m^2}>0$, $1-2m^2=0$, so $m^2=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $m=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ $(m>0)$.

Nature test: the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{dm}$ is decided by $1-2m^2$.

\extable{Ts4932_1}

$$\therefore\ m=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\text{ gives the maximum area}$$
criteria: Finds $m=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ without testing its nature, or equivalent merit
Differentiates the area correctly, or equivalent merit
Writes the area as $A=2me^{-m^2}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Given that $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, simplify the expression below as a single trigonometric ratio,

$$\sqrt{1+\sin^2 x+\sin^4 x+\sin^6 x+\dots}$$

solutions.latex:
The terms $1+\sin^2 x+\sin^4 x+\sin^6 x+\dots$ form a GP with $a=1$ and $r=\sin^2 x$.

Since $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $0\le\sin^2 x<1$, so $|r|<1$ and the sum to infinity exists.

$$\begin{aligned}S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\\&=\dfrac{1}{1-\sin^2 x}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\cos^2 x}\\&=\sec^2 x\end{aligned}$$

Hence $\sqrt{S_\infty}=\sqrt{\sec^2 x}=\sec x$, since $\cos x>0$ for $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ gives $\sec x>0$.

$$\therefore\ \sqrt{1+\sin^2 x+\sin^4 x+\sin^6 x+\dots}=\sec x$$
criteria: Identifies the GP and finds the sum to infinity, or equivalent merit

3447.stem:
An engineer models the rates of change of the amount of oil produced (in hundred barrels per day) by oil companies $A$ and $B$ respectively by

$$f'(t)=6\ln(t)\quad\text{and}\quad g'(t)=\dfrac{60t}{1+5t},$$

where $t$ is the number of days after some initial time $(2\leq t\leq 14)$.

parts.latex: Using the trapezoidal rule with 3 sub-intervals, estimate the total amount of oil produced by oil company $A$ from $t=2$ to $t=14$.

It can be shown that $\dfrac{5t}{1+5t}=1-\dfrac{1}{1+5t}$. DO NOT prove this.

Use this result to find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{60t}{1+5t}\,dt$.

The engineer claims that the total amount of oil produced by oil company $A$ from $t=2$ to $t=14$, is less than that of oil company $B$. Do you agree?

Justify your answer.

solutions.latex:
Using the trapezoidal rule with 3 sub-intervals, the strip width is

$$h=\dfrac{14-2}{3}=4$$

so the $t$ values are $2,6,10,14$.

$$\begin{aligned}\int_2^{14}f'(t)\,dt&\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\Big[f'(2)+f'(14)+2\big(f'(6)+f'(10)\big)\Big]\\&=2\Big[6\ln 2+6\ln 14+2\big(6\ln 6+6\ln 10\big)\Big]\\&\approx 138.25\end{aligned}$$

So company $A$ produced approximately 138.25 hundred barrels.
criteria: Applies the trapezoidal rule with correct $t$ values, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Since $60t=12\times 5t$, use the given result:

$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{60t}{1+5t}\,dt&=12\int\dfrac{5t}{1+5t}\,dt\\&=12\int\left(1-\dfrac{1}{1+5t}\right)dt\\&=12\left[t-\dfrac{1}{5}\ln(1+5t)\right]+C\\&=12t-\dfrac{12}{5}\ln(1+5t)+C\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Source wrote the constant as $C$ inside the bracket then $C_1$; merged into a single $C$ (same result).

solutions.latex:
Total oil produced by company $B$, using part (b):

$$\begin{aligned}\int_2^{14}\dfrac{60t}{1+5t}\,dt&=12\left[t-\dfrac{1}{5}\ln(1+5t)\right]_2^{14}\\&=12\left[14-\dfrac{1}{5}\ln(71)-2+\dfrac{1}{5}\ln(11)\right]\\&=12\left[12-\dfrac{1}{5}\ln\left(\dfrac{71}{11}\right)\right]\\&\approx 139.52\end{aligned}$$

So company $B$ produces approximately 139.52 hundred barrels, while from part (a) company $A$ produced approximately 138.25 hundred barrels.

On these estimates, company $B$ produces more.

However, the estimate for company $A$ used the trapezoidal rule. The graph of $\ln t$ is concave down, so the trapezoidal rule gives an underestimate, and the two values are very close.

So it is not possible to say from these values which company produces more oil over that period.

$$\therefore\ \text{We cannot agree or disagree with the engineer's claim from these values.}$$
criteria: Finds the total for company $B$ and compares it with the estimate for company $A$, or equivalent merit
Substitutes the limits into the integral from part (b), or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Source's conclusion kept: inconclusive because of the trapezoidal underestimate.

figures.cap: graphs of two normal distributions N1 and N2

solutions.latex:
A normal curve is centred on its mean, and a wider, flatter curve has the larger standard deviation.

From the graphs, $N_1$ is centred to the left of $N_2$, so $\mu_1<\mu_2$.

$N_1$ is wider and flatter than $N_2$, so $\sigma_1>\sigma_2$.

$$\therefore\ \mu_1<\mu_2 \text{ and } \sigma_1>\sigma_2$$

meta.format_note: Source gave only the statement of the answer; working written from the option and the usual reading of the graph (figure not seen). Check against figure 730_q1_1.

parts.latex:
The first term of an arithmetic sequence is 12. The fifteenth term of the same sequence is 67.

What is the common difference of the sequence?

solutions.latex:
For an arithmetic sequence $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ with $a=12$ and $T_{15}=67$.
$$\begin{aligned} 67&=12+14d\\ 14d&=55\\ d&=\dfrac{55}{14} \end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x)

solutions.latex:
Read the graph at $x=1$.

$f(1)\approx 1.5$

The curve is decreasing at $x=1$, so $f'(1)<0$.

The concavity changes at $x=1$, so $f''(1)\approx 0$.

Hence $f'(1)<f''(1)<f(1)$.

parts.latex: Which of the following expressions is equivalent to $\sec^2 x-\sin^2 x-\cos^2 x$ ?

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \sec^2 x-\sin^2 x-\cos^2 x&=\sec^2 x-(\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x)\\ &=\sec^2 x-1\\ &=\tan^2 x \end{aligned}$$
using $\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1$ and $\sec^2 x=1+\tan^2 x$.

parts.latex: What is the $10^{\text{th}}$ term of the sequence whose first 3 terms are 6144, 1536 and 384?

solutions.latex:
The terms are in a geometric sequence with $a=6144$.
$$r=\dfrac{1536}{6144}=\dfrac{1}{4}$$
Using $T_n=ar^{n-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} T_{10}&=6144\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^9\\ &=\dfrac{3}{128} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Options B, C and D each equal $\displaystyle\int_{-5}^{4} f(x)\,dx+\left|\displaystyle\int_{4}^{9} f(x)\,dx\right|$, which is the shaded area, since the region from $x=4$ to $x=9$ lies below the axis.

Option A: $\displaystyle\int_{-5}^{9} f(x)\,dx$ is the value of the definite integral, in which the negative region subtracts from the positive region.

parts.latex:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two events such that $P(X)=0.5$, $P(Y)=0.6$ and $P(Y\mid X)=0.7$

Which of the following statements is false?

solutions.latex:
Using $P(Y\mid X)=\dfrac{P(Y\cap X)}{P(X)}$:
$$\dfrac{P(Y\cap X)}{0.5}=0.7$$
so $P(Y\cap X)=0.35$, which makes C true.

For independence we need $P(X)\times P(Y)=P(X\cap Y)$.
$$P(X)\times P(Y)=0.5\times 0.6=0.3\neq 0.35$$
so $X$ and $Y$ are not independent, and statement B is false.

parts.latex:
Zane's grandparents put \$1200 in a savings account for him on the day of his birth and on every birthday until he turned 18. (The last deposit is made on his $18^{\text{th}}$ birthday.)

The account earns $2\%$ interest compounding annually.

If Zane withdraws the money on his $18^{\text{th}}$ birthday to pay for university, which expression gives the amount of money he will withdraw?

solutions.latex:
The deposits are made at ages $0,1,2,\dots,18$, and each earns interest until age 18.

The first deposit earns interest for 18 years and the last for 0 years.
$$\text{Total}=1200+1200(1.02)+1200(1.02)^2+\dots+1200(1.02)^{18}$$
This is a geometric series with $a=1200$, $r=1.02$ and 19 terms.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total}&=\dfrac{1200\left(1.02^{19}-1\right)}{1.02-1}\\ &=\dfrac{1200\left(1.02^{19}-1\right)}{0.02} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)=2-x$ and $g(x)=6+x$.

What is the domain of the function $h(x)=\ln\left\{\dfrac{f(-x)}{g(-x)}\right\}$ ?

solutions.latex:
Replacing $x$ by $-x$:
$$f(-x)=2+x,\qquad g(-x)=6-x$$
so
$$h(x)=\ln\left(\dfrac{2+x}{6-x}\right)$$
The logarithm needs $\dfrac{2+x}{6-x}>0$, so the numerator and denominator are both positive or both negative.

Both negative needs $x<-2$ and $x>6$, which is impossible.

Both positive:
$$\begin{aligned} 2+x>0&\ \text{ so } x>-2\\ 6-x>0&\ \text{ so } x<6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ -2<x<6$$

meta.format_note: Added the both-negative case to justify the domain (same result as source).

parts.latex:
On a continuous function $f(x)$, $h$ is a positive number which represents the horizontal difference between two points on the function.

Which of the following would NOT give the derivative of $f(x)$?

solutions.latex:
Option A is the definition of the derivative.

Option B is the gradient of the line joining $\left(x-\dfrac{h}{2},f\left(x-\dfrac{h}{2}\right)\right)$ and $\left(x+\dfrac{h}{2},f\left(x+\dfrac{h}{2}\right)\right)$. As $h\to 0$ this gives the gradient of the tangent at $(x,f(x))$.

Option C is the gradient of the line joining $(x-h,f(x-h))$ and $(x,f(x))$. As $h\to 0$ this gives the gradient of the tangent at $(x,f(x))$.

Option D is the negative of option C, since $f(x-h)-f(x)=-\big(f(x)-f(x-h)\big)$.

So it equals $-f'(x)$, which is not the same as $f'(x)$.

parts.latex: Find: $\displaystyle\int \sqrt[3]{4x+7}\,dx$

solutions.latex:
Write the cube root as a power, then integrate using $\displaystyle\int (ax+b)^n\,dx=\dfrac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}+c$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int \sqrt[3]{4x+7}\,dx&=\displaystyle\int(4x+7)^{\frac{1}{3}}\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{(4x+7)^{\frac{4}{3}}}{\frac{4}{3}\times 4}+c\\ &=\dfrac{3}{16}(4x+7)^{\frac{4}{3}}+c \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Partial progress towards correct answer, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find: $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{6(x-4)}{x^2-8x}\,dx$

solutions.latex:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator, since $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2-8x)=2x-8$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int \dfrac{6(x-4)}{x^2-8x}\,dx&=3\displaystyle\int\dfrac{2x-8}{x^2-8x}\,dx\\ &=3\ln\left|x^2-8x\right|+c \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Partial progress towards correct answer, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A series is given as $1-3k+9k^2+\dots$

What is the value of $k$ if the series has a limiting sum of $\dfrac{3}{4}$ ?

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric with first term and common ratio
$$a=1,\qquad r=\dfrac{9k^2}{-3k}=-3k$$
The limiting sum is $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3}{4}&=\dfrac{1}{1-(-3k)}\\ \dfrac{3}{4}&=\dfrac{1}{1+3k}\\ 3+9k&=4\\ k&=\dfrac{1}{9} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Partial progress towards correct answer, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Check: $r=-\dfrac{1}{3}$, so $|r|<1$ and the limiting sum exists.

parts.latex:
A sector has an arc length $l$ of $2\pi$ cm and an area $A$ of $24\pi$ cm$^2$.

The radius of the sector is $r$ cm.

Find the central angle $\theta$ of the sector, in exact form.

solutions.latex:
Using the arc length formula $l=r\theta$:
$$2\pi=r\theta,\quad\text{so } r=\dfrac{2\pi}{\theta}$$
Using the sector area formula $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} 24\pi&=\dfrac{r^2\theta}{2}\\ 48\pi&=r^2\theta \end{aligned}$$
Substituting $r=\dfrac{2\pi}{\theta}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 48\pi&=\dfrac{4\pi^2}{\theta^2}\times\theta\\ 48\pi\theta&=4\pi^2\\ \theta&=\dfrac{\pi}{12} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$$
criteria: Correct solution with only one error, or equivalent merit
Forms one correct equation, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the area equation is $24\pi=\dfrac{r^2\theta}{2}$ (the source dropped $\pi$), giving $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$, not $\dfrac{\pi^2}{12}$.
meta.format_note: Source error fixed: it wrote $24=\dfrac{r^2\theta}{2}$ (dropping $\pi$) and got $\theta=\dfrac{\pi^2}{12}$. Check: $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$ gives $r=24$, $A=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 576\times\dfrac{\pi}{12}=24\pi$.

parts.latex: Simplify fully: $(2\cos x+3\sin x)^2+(3\cos x-2\sin x)^2$

solutions.latex:
Expand each square.
$$\begin{aligned} &(2\cos x+3\sin x)^2+(3\cos x-2\sin x)^2\\ &=4\cos^2x+12\cos x\sin x+9\sin^2x+9\cos^2x-12\cos x\sin x+4\sin^2x\\ &=13\cos^2x+13\sin^2x\\ &=13(\sin^2x+\cos^2x)\\ &=13 \end{aligned}$$
using $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$.
criteria: Partial progress towards correct answer, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The share price (\$$P$) of a renewable energy company is increasing such that $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{3}{t+1}$, where $t$ is the time in months.

If the initial price of the share price is \$2.00, find the price after 6 months. Write your answer to the nearest cent.

solutions.latex:
Integrate the rate of change to find $P$.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=\displaystyle\int\dfrac{3}{t+1}\,dt\\ &=3\ln|t+1|+c \end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $P=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=3\ln 1+c\\ c&=2 \end{aligned}$$
So $P=3\ln|t+1|+2$.

When $t=6$:
$$\begin{aligned} P&=3\ln 7+2\\ &\approx \$7.84 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct solution with only one error, or equivalent merit
Correct expression for $P$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\big(f(x)\,g(x)\big)$ when $x=4$
$\displaystyle\int_1^3 \big(g'(x)+5\big)\,dx$

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\big(f(x)g(x)\big)=f(x)g'(x)+g(x)f'(x)$.

When $x=4$, using the values from the table:
$$\begin{aligned} f(4)g'(4)+g(4)f'(4)&=3\times 4+(-5)\times 7\\ &=-23 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the product rule and attempts to use values from the table, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Integrate term by term, then apply the limits.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_1^3 \big(g'(x)+5\big)\,dx&=\big[g(x)+5x\big]_1^3\\ &=g(3)+15-\big(g(1)+5\big)\\ &=-1+15-2-5\\ &=7 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Show that the derivative of $\dfrac{2x}{3x^2+1}$ is $\dfrac{2-6x^2}{(3x^2+1)^2}$

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=3x^2+1\\ u'&=2 & v'&=6x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{2(3x^2+1)-2x(6x)}{(3x^2+1)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{6x^2+2-12x^2}{(3x^2+1)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{2-6x^2}{(3x^2+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct expressions for $u'$ and $v'$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A cylinder contains water at an initial depth of 10cm. Water is poured into the cylinder such that the height increases by 10cm in the $1^{\text{st}}$ second, an additional 15 cm in $2^{\text{nd}}$ second, an additional 20cm in the $3^{\text{rd}}$ second and so on.

Assuming the cylinder has sufficient capacity, what would be the depth of water after 10 seconds.

solutions.latex:
The initial depth is $10$ cm. The increases $10, 15, 20, \dots$ form an arithmetic series with $a=10$, $d=5$, $n=10$.

Using the sum of an arithmetic series:
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{n}{2}\{2a+(n-1)d\} \\ S_{10} &= \dfrac{10}{2}\{20+(10-1)\cdot 5\} \\ &= 325 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
Add the initial depth:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Final depth} &= 325+10 \\ &= 335 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Calculates the correct increase in depth of water, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Differentiate $e^{x^2}$
Hence or otherwise evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^2 x e^{x^2}\,dx$

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule with $y=e^{x^2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= e^{x^2}\cdot 2x \\ &= 2xe^{x^2} \end{aligned}$$

From part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x^2}\right)=2xe^{x^2}$, so $xe^{x^2}$ is half of that derivative.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_0^2 xe^{x^2}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^2 2xe^{x^2}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[e^{x^2}\right]_0^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[e^4-e^0\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(e^4-1\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct primitive function, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that the graph of $y=f(x)$ has no stationary points.
Find any points of inflexion.
Sketch the graph $y=f(x)$, labelling any points of inflexion and all intercepts with the axes.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate:
$$f'(x)=3x^2+2x+3$$
Stationary points need $f'(x)=0$, that is $3x^2+2x+3=0$.

The discriminant is
$$\begin{aligned} \Delta &= 2^2-4(3)(3) \\ &= -32 \\ &< 0 \end{aligned}$$
So the equation has no real solutions.

$\therefore f(x)$ has no stationary points.

Differentiate again:
$$f''(x)=6x+2$$
Possible inflexions need $f''(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6x+2 &= 0 \\ x &= -\dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Then
$$f\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)=\dfrac{56}{27}$$
Test the concavity either side of $x=-\dfrac{1}{3}$:

\extable{Ts4967_1}

Since $f''(x)$ changes sign, there is a point of inflexion.

$$\therefore\ \text{point of inflexion at } \left(-\dfrac{1}{3},\dfrac{56}{27}\right)$$
criteria: Correct $x$ value, no change in concavity shown, or equivalent merit

criteria: Correct graph showing correct concavity and point of inflexion, or equivalent merit
Correct intercepts and correct shape, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: solution sketch: triangle ABC with sides 12, 20, 28

parts.latex:
In triangle ABC: AB = 12cm, BC = 20cm and AC = 28cm.

Find the exact area of the triangle.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{730_q25_s1}

Let $\beta=\angle ABC$. By the cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\beta &= \dfrac{12^2+20^2-28^2}{2\times 12\times 20} \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
So $\beta=120^\circ$.

Using the area formula $A=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 12\times 20\times\sin 120^\circ \\ &= 120\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &= 60\sqrt{3} \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, let $\alpha=\angle BAC$. By the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\alpha &= \dfrac{12^2+28^2-20^2}{2\times 12\times 28} \\ &= \dfrac{11}{14} \end{aligned}$$
By Pythagoras in a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $14$ and adjacent side $11$, $\sin\alpha=\dfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{14}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 12\times 28\times\sin\alpha \\ &= 6\times 28\times\dfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{14} \\ &= 60\sqrt{3} \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct exact sine ratio or correct area approximation (inverse-sine notation etc. not allowed), or equivalent merit
Correct exact cosine ratio for non-right triangle, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Sketch the graph of $y=f(x)$, showing any intercepts and asymptotes.
Show that the cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$.
Let the random variable $X$ represent the wait time, in minutes, until a new customer enters a shop. The probability density function of $X$ is exponential with $\lambda=\dfrac{1}{5}$.
Find the probability that the wait time until the next customer is more than 5 minutes, i.e. $P(X>5)$.

parts.latex:
Show that if a customer has not entered the shop in the last 5 minutes, the probability that it will take at least another 5 minutes for a customer to enter remains the same as in part (c) (i).

That is, show $P(X>10\mid X>5)=P(X>5)$.

solutions.latex: \exfigure{730_q26_s1}
criteria: Correct curve with a closed $y$-intercept dot but no $y=0$ for $x<0$, or equivalent merit
Increasing exponential curve, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Figure 730_q26_s1 must show: exponential decay curve for x >= 0 starting at (0, lambda) with a closed dot; y = 0 for x < 0 with an open circle at the origin; horizontal asymptote y = 0 labelled. Source rubric: 1 mark correct exponential curve, 1 mark correct intercept, 1 mark for y = 0.

solutions.latex:
For a PDF $f(x)$ with domain $a\le x\le b$, the CDF is
$$F(x)=P(X\le x)=\displaystyle\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$$
Here the domain starts at $0$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \displaystyle\int_0^x \lambda e^{-\lambda t}\,dt \\ &= \left[-e^{-\lambda t}\right]_0^x \\ &= -e^{-\lambda x}+1 \\ &= 1-e^{-\lambda x} \end{aligned}$$
More formally,
$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0 & x<0\\ 1-e^{-\lambda x} & x\ge 0\end{cases}$$
criteria: Correct integral expression for $F(x)$ or correct primitive, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source wrote the integrand and limit with the same letter x; a dummy variable t was used for the integration.

solutions.latex:
With $\lambda=\dfrac{1}{5}$, the CDF is $F(x)=1-e^{-\frac{x}{5}}$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X>5) &= 1-P(X<5) \\ &= 1-\left(1-e^{-\frac{5}{5}}\right) \\ &= 1-\left(1-e^{-1}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{e} \end{aligned}$$

First find $P(X>10)$ using $F(x)=1-e^{-\frac{x}{5}}$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(X>10) &= 1-\left(1-e^{-\frac{10}{5}}\right) \\ &= e^{-2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{e^2} \end{aligned}$$
Using conditional probability, and noting that $X>10$ already implies $X>5$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(X>10\mid X>5) &= \dfrac{P(X>10 \text{ and } X>5)}{P(X>5)} \\ &= \dfrac{P(X>10)}{P(X>5)} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{e^2}\div\dfrac{1}{e} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{e} \\ &= P(X>5) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $P(X>10)$ or divides by $P(X>5)$ $\left(\dfrac{1}{e}\right)$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $1-\tan x=\sin x-\sin x\tan x$ for $[0,2\pi]$

solutions.latex:
Bring all terms to one side:
$$\sin x-\sin x\tan x-1+\tan x=0$$
Factorise by grouping:
$$\begin{aligned} \sin x(1-\tan x)-(1-\tan x) &= 0 \\ (\sin x-1)(1-\tan x) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
By the Null Factor Law, $\sin x=1$ or $\tan x=1$.

For $\sin x=1$, $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. This does not satisfy the original equation, because $\tan\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is undefined.

For $\tan x=1$ in $[0,2\pi]$:
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{4}$$
criteria: Finds $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and then rules it out, or equivalent merit
Factorises (takes out $\sin x$ as a common factor), or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Most students found this difficult. Dividing both sides by $1-\tan x$ assumes $1-\tan x\neq 0$; instead bring all terms to the LHS, factorise and use the Null Factor Law. Check solutions by substituting back, as $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ does not satisfy the original equation because $\tan\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is undefined.

meta.format_note: Original single-row rubric text is kept in the source.

parts.latex:
The seats in a theatre are numbered in numerical order from the first row to the last row.

The first row has 14 seats. Each successive row has 4 more seats than the previous one.

If the theatre has a maximum capacity of 1320 seats, what is the greatest number of rows of seats in the theatre?

solutions.latex:
The seat numbers form an arithmetic series $14+18+\dots$ with $a=14$, $d=4$.

The total number of seats in $n$ rows is
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right] \\ &= \dfrac{n}{2}\left[2(14)+4(n-1)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{n}{2}(24+4n) \\ &= 12n+2n^2 \end{aligned}$$
The capacity is $1320$, so we need $S_n\le 1320$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2n^2+12n-1320 &\le 0 \\ n^2+6n-660 &\le 0 \end{aligned}$$
By the quadratic formula, the roots are
$$\begin{aligned} n &= \dfrac{-6\pm\sqrt{6^2-4(1)(-660)}}{2(1)} \\ &\approx -28.8 \text{ or } 22.8 \end{aligned}$$
Since $n>0$, $S_n\le 1320$ when $n\le 22.8$, and $n$ is a whole number.

Note: $S_{23}$ is a little more than $1320$ and $S_{22}$ is a little less than $1320$.

$$\therefore\ n=22 \text{ is the greatest number of rows.}$$
criteria: Correct expression for $n$, or equivalent merit
Correct expression for $S_n$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the centre and radius of the circle $x^2-2x+y^2-4y-15=0$.

solutions.latex:
Complete the square in $x$ and $y$:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2-2x+y^2-4y &= 15 \\ (x-1)^2+(y-2)^2 &= 15+1+4 \\ &= 20 \end{aligned}$$
The circle has centre $(1,2)$ and radius $\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt{5}$.

solutions.latex:
Let $P$ be the point on the circle furthest from the origin $O$.

\exfigure{730_q30_s1}

$O(0,0)$, $C(1,2)$ and $P$ must be collinear; if not, the distance $OP$ would be shorter than $OC+CP$.

The line through $O$ and $C$ has gradient $2$, so it is $y=2x$. Solve simultaneously with the circle:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2-2x+(2x)^2-4(2x) &= 15 \\ 5x^2-10x &= 15 \\ x^2-2x-3 &= 0 \\ (x-3)(x+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=3$ or $x=-1$. The furthest point has $x>0$ (on the far side of $C$ from $O$), so $x=3$ and $y=6$.

$$\therefore\ P=(3,6)$$
Alternative method:

\exfigure{730_q30_s2}

$OC=\sqrt{1^2+2^2}=\sqrt{5}$ and $PC=2\sqrt{5}$ (radius).

In the right-angled triangle with $AC=2$ and $OA=1$:
$$\tan\angle COA=\dfrac{AC}{OA}=\dfrac{2}{1}$$
So $\angle COA=\tan^{-1}2\ (\approx 63.43^\circ)$, and $\angle PCB=\tan^{-1}2$ (corresponding angles on parallel lines).

In the right-angled triangle $PBC$:
$$\begin{aligned} PB &= 2\sqrt{5}\sin(\tan^{-1}2) = 4 \\ BC &= 2\sqrt{5}\cos(\tan^{-1}2) = 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P=(1+2,\,2+4)=(3,6)$$

3479.stem:
John wants to accrue an investment of \$500 000 for his retirement in 30 years. He proposes to make a payment at the beginning of each year for the next 30 years.

The interest rate is set at $5\%$ p.a. At the end of $n$ years after starting his payments, the amount in the fund is $A_n$.

Let his first payment be \$$M$.

parts.latex: Show that $A_{30}=M\times 21\times(1.05^{30}-1)$
Hence, calculate the annual payment $M$.
After 20 years, John is able to increase his payment to \$8000 per year. What will be the new value of his investment at the end of the 30-year period?

solutions.latex:
Interest is $5\%$ p.a., so each year the amount is multiplied by $R=1.05$. Payments are made at the start of each year.
$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= M(1.05) \\ A_2 &= \left[M(1.05)+M\right](1.05) \\ &= M(1.05)^2+M(1.05) \\ A_3 &= \left[M(1.05)^2+M(1.05)+M\right](1.05) \\ &= M(1.05)^3+M(1.05)^2+M(1.05) \end{aligned}$$
Continuing the pattern,
$$A_{30}=M\left[1.05+1.05^2+1.05^3+\dots+1.05^{30}\right]$$
This is a geometric series with $a=1.05$, $r=1.05$ and $30$ terms. Using $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{30} &= M\left\{1.05\cdot\dfrac{1.05^{30}-1}{1.05-1}\right\} \\ &= M\left(\dfrac{1.05}{0.05}\right)\left(1.05^{30}-1\right) \\ &= M\times 21\times\left(1.05^{30}-1\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Obtains correct expressions for $A_1$, $A_2$ and $A_3$ and attempts to form an expression for $A_{30}$, or starts at a correct expression for $A_{30}$ and correctly simplifies, or equivalent merit
Obtains correct expressions for $A_1$ and $A_2$, or forms a correct expression for $A_{30}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Set $A_{30}=500\,000$ in the result from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} M &= \dfrac{500\,000}{21\left(1.05^{30}-1\right)} \\ &\approx \$7167.35 \end{aligned}$$

For a constant payment $M$, $A_n=M(21)\left(1.05^n-1\right)$.

After $20$ years, with $M=\$7167.35$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{20} &= 7167.35(21)\left(1.05^{20}-1\right) \\ &\approx \$248\,845.03 \end{aligned}$$
This grows for a further $10$ years, using $A=PR^n$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{10} &= 248\,845.03(1.05)^{10} \\ &\approx \$405\,342.33 \end{aligned}$$
The new payments of $M=\$8000$ for $10$ years give
$$\begin{aligned} A_{10} &= 8000(21)\left(1.05^{10}-1\right) \\ &\approx \$105\,654.30 \end{aligned}$$
Add the two amounts:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total} &= \$405\,342.33+\$105\,654.30 \\ &= \$510\,996.63 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Obtains correct values for two of $A_{10}$, $A_{20}$ or $A_{30}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show $DC=2\sin\theta$.
Hence, or otherwise show that the area of the triangle $\triangle ABC$ is given by $A=4\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)$.
Find the value of $\theta$ that maximises the area of $\triangle ABC$.

solutions.latex:
In the right-angled $\triangle ODC$, $OC=2$ (radius), so
$$\sin\theta=\dfrac{DC}{OC}=\dfrac{DC}{2}$$
$$\therefore\ DC=2\sin\theta$$

Use $A=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\text{base}\times\text{height}$.

The base is $BC=2\,DC=4\sin\theta$ (using part (a)).

The height is $AD=OD+OA=2\cos\theta+2$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 4\sin\theta\times(2+2\cos\theta) \\ &= 4\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta) \end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=4\sin\theta & v&=1+\cos\theta\\ u'&=4\cos\theta & v'&=-\sin\theta\end{aligned}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{d\theta} &= 4\cos\theta(1+\cos\theta)-4\sin^2\theta \\ &= 4\cos^2\theta-4\sin^2\theta+4\cos\theta \\ &= 4\left(\cos^2\theta-\left(1-\cos^2\theta\right)+\cos\theta\right) \\ &= 4\left(2\cos^2\theta+\cos\theta-1\right) \\ &= 4(2\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+1) \end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=0$, so $\cos\theta=-1$ or $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Then $\theta=180^\circ$ or $\theta=60^\circ$. Since $\theta$ is acute, $\theta=60^\circ$.

Check that it is a maximum:

\extable{Ts4987_1}

$$\therefore\ \text{the area is a maximum when } \theta=60^\circ$$
criteria: Correct value but does not check it is a maximum, or equivalent merit
Applies trig identities and factorises correctly, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: graph of y = sin 2x - x with a double tangent line through A and B and shaded region between

solutions.latex:
Let $f(x)=\sin 2x-x$. Then
$$f'(x)=2\cos 2x-1$$
At $B$, $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, so the gradient of the tangent is
$$\begin{aligned} f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) &= 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}-1 \\ &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
and
$$\begin{aligned} f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) &= \sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{4} \\ &= 1-\dfrac{\pi}{4} \end{aligned}$$
The tangent is
$$\begin{aligned} y-\left(1-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) &= -\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \\ y &= 1-x \end{aligned}$$
The tangent meets the curve where
$$\begin{aligned} 1-x &= \sin 2x-x \\ \sin 2x &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
So $2x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ or $2x=-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$, giving $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ (point $B$) or $x=-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ (point $A$).

The line is above the curve between $A$ and $B$, so the shaded area is
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \displaystyle\int_{-\frac{3\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left[(1-x)-(\sin 2x-x)\right]dx \\ &= \displaystyle\int_{-\frac{3\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(1-\sin 2x)\,dx \\ &= \left[x+\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x\right]_{-\frac{3\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &= \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\dfrac{1}{2}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)-\left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}+\dfrac{1}{2}\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{4}+\dfrac{3\pi}{4} \\ &= \pi \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct progress up to the correct antiderivative for the area with endpoints, or equivalent merit
Correct progress up to the correct $x$ coordinate of point $A$, or equivalent merit
Correct progress up to the correct equation of the tangent, or equivalent merit
Correct gradient of the tangent, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A discrete probability distribution is given by:

$$P(X=x) = \begin{cases} kx & \text{for } x = 1,2,3,4 \\ 0 & \text{for any other } x \text{ value} \end{cases}$$

Which statement is false?

solutions.latex:
For $x=2$, the rule $P(X=x)=kx$ gives
$$P(X=2)=k\times 2=2k$$
This is not equal to $2x$, so statement B is false.

Which combination of $a$ and $c$ can possibly produce a situation in which the graphs of $f(x) = ax^2$ and $g(x) = x + c$ do not cross?

parts.latex:
What transformations have been carried out to go from $y = f(x)$ to $y = g(x)$?

These must be written in the correct order?

solutions.latex:
Take the transformations in order, horizontal first, then vertical.

Step 1: replace $x$ with $2x$.
$$h(x)=f(2x)=(2x-2)^2$$
So $f(x)$ is dilated horizontally by a scale factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Step 2: replace $x$ with $x+\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} k(x)&=h\left(x+\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &=\left(2\left(x+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-2\right)^2 \\ &=(2x-1)^2 \end{aligned}$$
So $h(x)$ is translated left by $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Step 3: subtract 2.
$$\begin{aligned} g(x)&=k(x)-2 \\ &=(2x-1)^2-2 \\ &=4x^2-4x-1 \end{aligned}$$
So $k(x)$ is translated down by 2.

A biased coin is tossed. The probability that it lands showing heads is 0.3.

To play a game, the coin is tossed 3 times.

Find the probability that, in the game, 3 heads are tossed given that at least one of the tosses is a head.
How many times would the coin need to be tossed so that the probability of getting at least one head will exceed 98%?

solutions.latex:
Each toss has $P(H)=0.3$ and $P(T)=0.7$, so each branch of the tree is labelled with these.

The sample space is HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT.
$$P(HHH)=0.3^3=0.027$$
$$P(TTT)=0.7^3=0.343$$

\exfigure{460_q8_s1}
criteria: Draws part of the tree correctly, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw: three-stage probability tree, each branch H with 0.3 and T with 0.7, eight outcomes HHH to TTT with probabilities at the ends (HHH 0.027, TTT 0.343). Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Using conditional probability:
$$\begin{aligned} P(3H \mid \text{at least 1 head}) &= \dfrac{P(3H \cap \text{at least 1 head})}{P(\text{at least 1 head})} \\ &= \dfrac{0.027}{1-0.343} \\ &\approx 0.0411 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the correct conditional probability ratio, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
For $n$ tosses, $P(\text{at least 1 head})=1-0.7^n$.

We need this to exceed $0.98$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1-0.7^n &> 0.98 \\ 0.02 &> 0.7^n \\ \log 0.02 &> n\log 0.7 \end{aligned}$$
Since $\log 0.7<0$, dividing reverses the inequality.
$$n>\dfrac{\log 0.02}{\log 0.7}\approx 10.97$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the coin must be tossed at least 11 times}$$
criteria: Sets up and solves $0.7^n<0.02$ with an error, or equivalent merit

Let $f(x)=2-x$ and $g(x)=6+x$.

What is the domain of the function $h(x)=\log_e\left(\dfrac{f(-x)}{g(-x)}\right)$?

solutions.latex:
Replacing $x$ by $-x$,
$$f(-x)=2+x,\qquad g(-x)=6-x$$
so
$$h(x)=\log_e\left(\dfrac{2+x}{6-x}\right)$$
A logarithm needs a positive argument, so
$$\dfrac{2+x}{6-x}>0$$
The quotient is positive when numerator and denominator have the same sign.

parts.latex: A series is given as $1-3k+9k^2+\dots$, what is the value of $k$ if the sum to infinity is $\dfrac{3}{4}$?

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric with first term $a=1$ and common ratio $r=-3k$.

A sum to infinity exists only when $|r|<1$, and then
$$S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}=\dfrac{1}{1+3k}$$
Set this equal to $\dfrac{3}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{1+3k} &= \dfrac{3}{4} \\ 1+3k &= \dfrac{4}{3} \\ 3k &= \dfrac{1}{3} \\ k &= \dfrac{1}{9} \end{aligned}$$
Check: $r=-\dfrac{1}{3}$, so $|r|<1$ and the sum exists.

Hence the correct option is C.

parts.latex:
The straight lines shown below $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ have equations $x+ay=b$ and $x+cy=d$ respectively. Which of the following are true?

I. $a<c$

II. $b>d$

III. $a+b<c+d$

\exfigure{1337_q10_1}

solutions.latex:
Write each line as $y=-\dfrac{1}{a}x+\dfrac{b}{a}$, so its gradient is $-\dfrac{1}{a}$ and its $y$-intercept is $\dfrac{b}{a}$. The other line has gradient $-\dfrac{1}{c}$ and $y$-intercept $\dfrac{d}{c}$.

Both lines have positive gradient, so $a<0$ and $c<0$.

Statement I: $\ell_2$ is steeper than $\ell_1$, so $\dfrac{1}{|c|}>\dfrac{1}{|a|}$, that is $|a|>|c|$. Since both are negative, $a<c$. True.

Statement II: for $\ell_1$ the $y$-intercept is $-1$, so $\dfrac{b}{a}=-1$ and $b=-a>0$.

$\ell_2$ crosses the $x$-axis left of the origin and rises, so its $y$-intercept $\dfrac{d}{c}$ is positive. With $c<0$ this gives $d<0$.

Hence $b>0>d$. True.

Statement III: $a+b=a+(-a)=0$, while $c+d$ is negative (both $c<0$ and $d<0$).

So $a+b>c+d$. False.

$$\therefore\ \text{I and II only}$$
Hence the correct option is A.

3513.stem: The seats in a theatre are numbered in numerical order from the first row to the last row. The first row has 14 seats. Each successive row has 4 more seats than the previous one.

solutions.latex:
The rows form an arithmetic sequence with $a=14$ and $d=4$.
$$\begin{aligned}T_4&=14+(4-1)\times4\\ &=26\end{aligned}$$
There are $26$ seats in row 4.

The total seats is the sum of an arithmetic series, $S_n=\dfrac n2\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$.
$$\begin{aligned}1320&=\dfrac n2\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)\\ 1320&=\dfrac n2(28+4n-4)\\ 2640&=n(24+4n)\\ 4n^2+24n-2640&=0\end{aligned}$$
As $n>0$, take the positive root.
$$\begin{aligned}n&=\dfrac{-24+\sqrt{24^2-4(4)(-2640)}}{2(4)}\\ &\approx 22.865\end{aligned}$$
$n$ must be a whole number not exceeding this, so $n=22$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the greatest number of rows is } 22$$

3522.stem: John's grandfather wishes to leave him \$250,000 in his will. He proposes to make a payment to an insurance company at the beginning of each year up until his death. Show that $A_{30}=R\left[\dfrac{1.07^{31}-1}{0.07}\right]$.
Hence, calculate the annual payment.

solutions.latex:
Each year the fund grows by 7%, and a payment of $R$ is added at the start of the year.
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=1.07A_0=1.07R\\ A_2&=(A_1+R)\times1.07\\ &=1.07^2R+1.07R\end{aligned}$$

Continuing in the same way:
$$\begin{aligned}A_3&=(A_2+R)\times1.07\\ &=1.07^3R+1.07^2R+1.07R\\ &\ \vdots\\ A_{30}&=1.07^{30}R+\dots+1.07^2R+1.07R\end{aligned}$$
The payout happens immediately after the last payment, so one more $R$ is added:
$$\begin{aligned}A_{30}&=1.07^{30}R+\dots+1.07^2R+1.07R+R\\ &=R\left[1.07^{30}+\dots+1.07+1\right]\end{aligned}$$
This is a geometric series with $a=1$, $r=1.07$ and $31$ terms (powers $0$ to $30$), so
$$A_{30}=R\left[\dfrac{1.07^{31}-1}{0.07}\right]$$
criteria: Progress towards solution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Solve the following simultaneous equation.

$\log_8 y=x-2$

$3(\log_8 y)^2=5-2x$

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}\log_8y&=x-2 &&(1)\\ 3(\log_8y)^2&=5-2x &&(2)\end{aligned}$$
Substitute (1) into (2):
$$\begin{aligned}3(x-2)^2&=5-2x\\ 3(x^2-4x+4)&=5-2x\\ 3x^2-12x+12&=5-2x\\ 3x^2-10x+7&=0\\ (3x-7)(x-1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=\dfrac73$ or $x=1$.

Substitute back into (1):
$$\begin{aligned}\log_8y&=\dfrac73-2=\dfrac13 &&\text{so } y=8^{\frac13}=2\\ \log_8y&=1-2=-1 &&\text{so } y=8^{-1}=\dfrac18\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \left(\dfrac73,\,2\right)\text{ and }\left(1,\,\dfrac18\right)$$
criteria: Solves the quadratic correctly, or equivalent merit
Forms the quadratic equation, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that the graph of $y=f(x)$ has no stationary points.

solutions.latex:
Stationary points need $f'(x)=0$.
$$f'(x)=3x^2+2x+3$$
The discriminant of $3x^2+2x+3=0$ is
$$\begin{aligned}\Delta&=2^2-4(3)(3)\\ &=-32<0\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore f'(x)=0$ has no solution, so $f(x)$ has no stationary points.
criteria: Differentiates correctly and attempts to solve $f'(x)=0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
A point of inflexion needs $f''(x)=0$ with a change in concavity.
$$\begin{aligned}f''(x)&=6x+2=0\\ x&=-\dfrac13\end{aligned}$$
$$f\left(-\dfrac13\right)=\dfrac{56}{27}$$
\extable{Ts5050_1}

Since $f''(x)$ changes sign, there is a point of inflexion at
$$\left(-\dfrac13,\dfrac{56}{27}\right)$$
criteria: Finds $f''(x)$ and solves $f''(x)=0$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A continuous random variable $X$ has a probability density function $f$ given

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}Ax+B & 1\le x\le 7\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants. The median is 3. Find the values of $A$ and $B$.

solutions.latex:
The total area under the density is 1, and half the area lies below the median $3$.
$$\int_1^7(Ax+B)\,dx=1 \quad (1),\qquad \int_1^3(Ax+B)\,dx=\dfrac12 \quad (2)$$
Evaluating (1):
$$\left[\dfrac{Ax^2}{2}+Bx\right]_1^7=1,\quad\text{so}\quad 24A+6B=1 \quad (1)$$
Evaluating (2):
$$\left[\dfrac{Ax^2}{2}+Bx\right]_1^3=\dfrac12,\quad\text{so}\quad 4A+2B=\dfrac12 \quad (2)$$
Multiply (2) by 3:
$$12A+6B=\dfrac32 \quad (3)$$
Subtract (3) from (1):
$$12A=-\dfrac12,\quad\text{so}\quad A=-\dfrac{1}{24}$$
Then $B=\dfrac13$.
$$\therefore\ A=-\dfrac{1}{24},\quad B=\dfrac13$$
criteria: Creates correct simultaneous equations, or equivalent merit
Creates one correct integral, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 4}\dfrac{x^2-2x-8}{\sqrt{x}-2}$.

solutions.latex:
Factorise the numerator and rationalise the denominator:
$$\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to4}\dfrac{x^2-2x-8}{\sqrt x-2}&=\lim_{x\to4}\dfrac{(x+2)(x-4)}{\sqrt x-2}\times\dfrac{\sqrt x+2}{\sqrt x+2}\\ &=\lim_{x\to4}\dfrac{(x+2)(x-4)(\sqrt x+2)}{x-4}\\ &=\lim_{x\to4}(x+2)(\sqrt x+2)\\ &=(4+2)(\sqrt4+2)\\ &=24\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Rationalises the denominator and factorises the quadratic, or equivalent merit
Rationalises the denominator or factorises the quadratic, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that the area of the triangle $\triangle ABC$ is given by $A=4\sin\theta\,(1+\cos\theta)$.
can_use: Area of a triangle (½ab sin C)

parts.latex: Find the value of $\theta$ that maximises the area of $\triangle ABC$.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1337_q34_s1}

In $\triangle ODC$, using trig ratios:
$$\sin\theta=\dfrac x2,\quad \cos\theta=\dfrac y2$$
so $x=2\sin\theta$ and $y=2\cos\theta$.

The base of $\triangle ABC$ is $b=2x=4\sin\theta$ and its height is $h=2+y=2+2\cos\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{bh}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{4\sin\theta(2+2\cos\theta)}{2}\\ &=4\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Progress towards solution, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Solution diagram 1337_q34_s1 is referenced as in source; labels assumed already present.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=4\sin\theta & v&=1+\cos\theta\\ u'&=4\cos\theta & v'&=-\sin\theta\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}&=4\cos\theta(1+\cos\theta)-4\sin^2\theta\\ &=4\cos\theta+4\cos^2\theta-4(1-\cos^2\theta)\\ &=8\cos^2\theta+4\cos\theta-4\\ &=4(2\cos^2\theta+\cos\theta-1)\end{aligned}$$
Set $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=0$:
$$(2\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+1)=0$$
So $\cos\theta=\dfrac12$, since $\cos\theta\ne-1$ for $0<\theta<\pi$. Hence $\theta=\dfrac\pi3$.

Test the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}$ either side:

\extable{Ts5055_1}

The derivative changes from positive to negative, so $\theta=\dfrac\pi3$ is a maximum.

The maximum area is
$$A\left(\dfrac\pi3\right)=4\sin\dfrac\pi3\left(1+\cos\dfrac\pi3\right)=3\sqrt3$$
$$\therefore\ \theta=\dfrac\pi3$$
criteria: Finds correct $\theta$ value, including testing nature, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The graph of $f(x)=3^{2x}-10\left(3^x\right)+9$ is shown below. Find the exact value of the area shaded.

\exfigure{1337_q35_1}

solutions.latex:
The curve meets the $x$-axis where $f(x)=0$. Let $u=3^x$:
$$\begin{aligned}u^2-10u+9&=0\\ (u-9)(u-1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $u=1$ or $u=9$, giving $3^x=1$ or $3^x=9$, hence $x=0$ or $x=2$.

The shaded region is below the $x$-axis, so the area is the absolute value of the integral:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\left|\int_0^2\left(3^{2x}-10\left(3^x\right)+9\right)dx\right|\\ &=\left|\left[\dfrac{3^{2x}}{2\ln3}-\dfrac{10\left(3^x\right)}{\ln3}+9x\right]_0^2\right|\\ &=\left|\left(\dfrac{3^4}{2\ln3}-\dfrac{10\left(3^2\right)}{\ln3}+18\right)-\left(\dfrac{3^0}{2\ln3}-\dfrac{10\left(3^0\right)}{\ln3}+0\right)\right|\\ &=\left|\dfrac{18\ln3-40}{\ln3}\right|\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=\dfrac{40-18\ln3}{\ln3}\ \text{units}^2$$
criteria: Correct substitution and makes progress towards solution, or equivalent merit
Correctly finds the primitive function, or equivalent merit
Sets up the correct integral to calculate the area, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Mr Kim recorded the time it took him to drive to work over five days. The mean time was $37$ minutes. The next workday it took Mr Kim $49$ minutes to drive to work. What is his new mean time?
parts.note: Mean of a raw data set (summary statistics) has no 2024 Advanced dot point; it is Standard data analysis content.

The total of the first five times is $37\times5$. Adding the sixth time gives the new mean.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{New mean} &= \dfrac{37\times5+49}{6} \\ &= 39 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
What is the equation of the graph shown below?

\exfigure{1338_q3_1}

solutions.latex:
The graph is an inverted V, so it has the form $f(x)=-a|x-h|+k$ with vertex $(h,k)$.

The vertex is at $(4,3)$, so $h=4$ and $k=3$.

The graph passes through $(0,-5)$. Substituting to find $a$:
$$\begin{aligned} -5 &= -a|0-4|+3 \\ -4a &= -8 \\ a &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
Check with the point $(2,-1)$ on the graph:
$$-2|2-4|+3=-4+3=-1$$
So the equation is
$$f(x)=-2|x-4|+3$$
Options A and C have $a=1$ (and C has the vertex at $x=-4$), and B has the vertex at $x=-4$, so only D fits.

parts.latex:
What type of relationship is represented by the graph shown below?

\exfigure{1338_q4_1}

solutions.latex:
The graph is the right half of the circle $x^2+y^2=16$, with $0\le x\le 4$ and $-4\le y\le 4$.

A vertical line $x=c$ with $0<c<4$ cuts the graph at two points, so one $x$ value gives two $y$ values.

A horizontal line $y=c$ cuts the graph at only one point, so each $y$ value comes from exactly one $x$ value.

So each $x$ is paired with many $y$ values, but each $y$ with only one $x$.

Therefore the relationship is one-to-many.

parts.latex: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{2}{3-x}$ and $g(x)=x-5$. The domain of $f(g(x))$ is

solutions.latex:
Substitute $g(x)$ into $f$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(g(x)) &= \dfrac{2}{3-(x-5)} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{3-x+5} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{-x+8} \end{aligned}$$
The denominator cannot be zero, so $-x+8\neq0$.

Hence $x\neq8$, which is option D.

parts.latex: The radius and centre of a circle with equation $x^2+y^2-8y-1=0$ is

solutions.latex:
Complete the square in $y$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2+y^2-8y-1 &= 0 \\ x^2+y^2-8y+\left(\dfrac{8}{2}\right)^2 &= \left(\dfrac{8}{2}\right)^2+1 \\ x^2+(y-4)^2 &= 17 \end{aligned}$$
So the centre is $(0,4)$ and the radius is $\sqrt{17}$, which is option D.

parts.latex: Find the derivative of $e^{x\cos3x}$.

solutions.latex:
For $y=e^{f(x)}$, $y'=f'(x)\,e^{f(x)}$, with $f(x)=x\cos3x$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\cos3x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-3\sin3x\end{aligned}$$
Then $f'(x)=\cos3x-3x\sin3x$.

So $y'=e^{x\cos3x}(\cos3x-3x\sin3x)$, which is option D.

parts.latex: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=x^3-4x^2$ at the point $(2,-8)$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate to find the gradient function.
$$y'=3x^2-8x$$
At $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} m &= 3(2)^2-8(2) \\ &= -4 \end{aligned}$$
Use the point-gradient form with $(2,-8)$.
$$\begin{aligned} y-(-8) &= -4(x-2) \\ y+8 &= -4x+8 \\ y &= -4x \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=-4x$$

parts.latex: Differentiate $\dfrac{x^3+2}{x-1}$.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^3+2 & v&=x-1\\ u'&=3x^2 & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x^3+2}{x-1}\right) &= \dfrac{3x^2(x-1)-(x^3+2)(1)}{(x-1)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{3x^3-3x^2-x^3-2}{(x-1)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{2x^3-3x^2-2}{(x-1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct quotient rule substitution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
What is the limiting sum of the following geometric series?

$$-324+108-36+12\dots$$

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric with $a=-324$ and common ratio
$$r=\dfrac{108}{-324}=-\dfrac{1}{3}$$
Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum is $S=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$.
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{-324}{1-\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)} \\ &= -243 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Solve $2\log_2 x-\log_2(x+6)=3$.

solutions.latex:
The logarithms need $x>0$ and $x+6>0$.

Apply the power law, then the quotient law.
$$\begin{aligned} \log_2x^2-\log_2(x+6) &= 3 \\ \log_2\dfrac{x^2}{x+6} &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
Convert to exponential form.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x^2}{x+6} &= 2^3 \\ x^2 &= 8(x+6) \\ x^2-8x-48 &= 0 \\ (x-12)(x+4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=12$ or $x=-4$.

Since $x>0$, reject $x=-4$.
$$\therefore\ x=12$$
criteria: Converts to exponential form, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Students forgot the last step.

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)dx$.

solutions.latex:
Write the integrand so that the factor $\dfrac{1}{3}$ from the derivative of the inner function appears.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)dx &= 3\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{1}{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)dx \\ &= 3\left[\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= 3\left[\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}-\sin0\right] \\ &= 3\left(\dfrac{1}{2}-0\right) \\ &= \dfrac{3}{2} \end{aligned}$$

3546.stem:
Mr Tan played a table tennis match. The number of points, $X$, that he scores in each set is a random variable with probability distribution given by:

\extable{1338_q18_t1}

parts.latex: Evaluate $a$ and $b$ given that Mr Tan has an expected score of $10.4$ per set.
Calculate the variance of $X$.

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to $1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.2+a+b+0.1 &= 1 \\ a+b &= 0.7 \\ a &= 0.7-b \end{aligned}$$
The expected value is $10.4$.
$$\begin{aligned} 9\times0.2+10a+11b+12\times0.1 &= 10.4 \\ 1.8+10a+11b+1.2 &= 10.4 \\ 10a+11b &= 7.4 \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $a=0.7-b$.
$$\begin{aligned} 10(0.7-b)+11b &= 7.4 \\ 7-10b+11b &= 7.4 \\ b &= 0.4 \end{aligned}$$
Then $a=0.7-0.4=0.3$.
$$\therefore\ a=0.3,\ b=0.4$$

meta.marker_note: If $a=0.3$ and $b=0.4$ are given with no working, maximum 1 mark.

solutions.latex:
Use $\text{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-\mu^2$ with $\mu=10.4$.
$$\begin{aligned} E(X^2) &= 81\times0.2+100\times0.3+121\times0.4+144\times0.1 \\ &= 109 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X) &= 109-10.4^2 \\ &= 109-108.16 \\ &= 0.84 \end{aligned}$$

3547.stem: A semi circle with radius $5$ has equation $f(x)=\sqrt{25-x^2}$.

parts.latex: Use the trapezoidal rule with five function values to approximate the area of the semi circle. Answer correct to $3$ decimal places.
Calculate the difference between the actual area of the semi circle and the approximation by the trapezoidal rule. Answer correct to $3$ decimal places.
Explain why the trapezoidal rule gives an estimate that is lower than the actual area of the semi circle.

solutions.latex:
Five function values means $n=4$ intervals, with $a=-5$ and $b=5$, so the strip width is $h=\dfrac{5-(-5)}{4}=2.5$.

The $x$ values are $-5,\,-2.5,\,0,\,2.5,\,5$, with
$$\begin{aligned} f(-5)&=0 & f(-2.5)&=\sqrt{18.75}\\ f(0)&=5 & f(2.5)&=\sqrt{18.75}\\ f(5)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Using the trapezoidal rule,
$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx \dfrac{b-a}{2n}\Big\{f(a)+f(b)+2\big[f(x_1)+f(x_2)+f(x_3)\big]\Big\} \\ &= \dfrac{5-(-5)}{2\times4}\Big\{0+0+2\big[\sqrt{18.75}+5+\sqrt{18.75}\big]\Big\} \\ &= 34.15063509\ldots \\ &\approx 34.151 \text{ units}^2 \text{ (3 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: The formula and a line of substitution must be written out.
meta.format_note: Added derivation of $n$ and strip width.

solutions.latex:
The semicircle has radius $5$, so its actual area is
$$A=\dfrac{1}{2}\pi\times5^2=\dfrac{25\pi}{2}=39.2699\ldots$$
The difference is
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{25\pi}{2}-34.151 &= 5.119 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
The trapezoidal rule gives the smaller value.

The graph of the semicircle is concave down.

So each chord joining two points on the curve lies below the curve, and every trapezium lies below the curve.

Hence the trapezoidal rule gives an estimate lower than the actual area.

parts.latex:
Mr Huynh recorded how many push ups he did each day for thirty days.

parts.note: Outliers (quartiles/IQR) of a data set are not in 2024 Advanced; they are Mathematics Standard content.

solutions.latex:
There are $30$ scores. The cumulative frequencies are $10, 16, 28, 29, 29, 29, 30$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Median} &= 15.5\text{th score} = 120 \\ Q_1 &= 8\text{th score} = 100 \\ Q_3 &= 23\text{rd score} = 140 \\ IQR &= 140-100 = 40 \end{aligned}$$
A value is an outlier if it is above $Q_3+1.5\times IQR$.
$$\begin{aligned} Q_3+1.5\times IQR &= 140+1.5\times40 \\ &= 200 \end{aligned}$$
Since $220>200$, $220$ push ups is an outlier.

parts.latex:
Mrs Briggs notices that the amount of emails she receives per week from students is cyclical. Every $12$ weeks she receives the highest number of emails. The average amount of emails per week is $25$ and the highest number of emails per week is $40$.

The number of emails Mrs Briggs receives each week, $f(t)$, is given by

$$f(t)=a\cos(bt)+c$$

where $t$ is the number of weeks after 1 January 2022 and $0\le t\le 52$.

The number of emails is at a maximum when $t=0$.

Find the values $a$, $b$ and $c$.

solutions.latex:
The maximum is at $t=0$, so the cosine form $f(t)=a\cos(bt)+c$ fits with $a>0$.

The period is $12$ weeks, and period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 12 &= \dfrac{2\pi}{b} \\ b &= \dfrac{\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$
The average is $25$, so the centre line is $c=25$.

The maximum is $40$, so the amplitude is $a=40-25=15$.
$$\therefore\ a=15,\ b=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ c=25$$
criteria: Finds two of $a$, $b$, $c$ correctly, or equivalent merit
Finds one of $a$, $b$, $c$ correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Currently, there is a mouse plague in Western NSW. The population of mice can be found using the formula $N=10\left(e^{kt}\right)$, where $N$ is the number of mice and $t$ is the time in months.

The plague started with $10$ mice and increased to $100$ mice after $3$ months.

By first finding the value of $k$, show that the exact rate of increase after $12$ months is $\dfrac{10\ln10}{3}\left(e^{\ln10000}\right)$ mice/month.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $N=100$ and $t=3$ into $N=10e^{kt}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 100&=10e^{3k}\\ 10&=e^{3k}\\ \ln 10&=3k\\ k&=\dfrac{\ln 10}{3} \end{aligned}$$
So $N=10e^{\frac{\ln 10}{3}t}$.

Differentiating, the rate of increase is
$$N'=10\times\dfrac{\ln 10}{3}e^{\frac{\ln 10}{3}t}$$
At $t=12$:
$$\begin{aligned} N'&=\dfrac{10\ln 10}{3}e^{\frac{\ln 10}{3}(12)}\\ &=\dfrac{10\ln 10}{3}e^{4\ln 10}\\ &=\dfrac{10\ln 10}{3}e^{\ln 10^4}\\ &=\dfrac{10\ln 10}{3}e^{\ln 10000} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ N'=\dfrac{10\ln 10}{3}\left(e^{\ln 10000}\right) \text{ mice/month}$$
criteria: Finds the derivative and substitutes $t=12$, or equivalent merit
Finds $k=\dfrac{\ln 10}{3}$ and the derivative, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Leave $k$ as an exact value; both of the last lines are needed for the final mark (this is a show question).

parts.latex: Prove that $\tan\theta\sin\theta+\cos\theta=\sec\theta$.

solutions.latex:
Using $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\tan\theta\sin\theta+\cos\theta\\ &=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\sin\theta+\cos\theta\\ &=\dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta}+\cos\theta\\ &=\dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta}+\dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\cos\theta}\\ &=\dfrac{\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta}{\cos\theta}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} &&(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1)\\ &=\sec\theta\\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes over a common denominator, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Sketch the graph of the curve $y=x^3-3x^2+1$, labelling the stationary points and point of inflection.

Do NOT determine the $x$-intercepts of the curve.

solutions.latex:
The $y$-intercept is $y=1$.

Stationary points occur when $y'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=3x^2-6x\\ &=3x(x-2)=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=2$.
$$y(0)=1,\qquad y(2)=2^3-3(2)^2+1=-3$$
Test the sign of $y'$:
$$\begin{aligned} x=-0.1,\,0,\,0.1:&\ y'=0.63,\,0,\,-0.57 &&\text{so } (0,1) \text{ is a maximum}\\ x=1.9,\,2,\,2.1:&\ y'=-0.57,\,0,\,0.63 &&\text{so } (2,-3) \text{ is a minimum} \end{aligned}$$
A possible point of inflection occurs when $y''=0$.
$$y''=6x-6=0,\quad x=1,\quad y=1-3+1=-1$$
Test the sign of $y''$:
$$x=0.9,\,1,\,1.1:\ y''=-0.6,\,0,\,0.6$$
The concavity changes from down to up, so $(1,-1)$ is a point of inflection.

\exfigure{1338_q26_s1}

3555.stem: Mr Pollard is creating a website. Every weekend, apart from the first, he adds the same number of pages to his website. After four weekends he has added $25$ pages and after eleven weekends he has added $74$ pages.

parts.latex:
Show that the total number amount of pages, $P$, added after the $n$th weekend can be modelled by the recurrence relation

$$P_n=P_{n-1}+7,\quad \text{where } n=2,3,4\dots$$
Given that on the first weekend he only added $4$ pages, use the recurrence relation to find the total number of pages Mr Pollard has added after the third weekend.

solutions.latex:
The common difference is found from $P_{11}=P_4+7d$.
$$\begin{aligned} 25+7d&=74\\ 7d&=49\\ d&=7 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P_n=P_{n-1}+7$$

Using the recurrence relation with the first weekend's $4$ pages:
$$\begin{aligned} P_0&=4\\ P_1&=4+7=11\\ P_2&=11+7=18 \end{aligned}$$
He has $18$ pages after the third weekend.

meta.marker_note: You must use the recurrence relation.
meta.format_note: The source indexes from $P_0$ for the first weekend while the recurrence in (a) starts at $n=2$; kept as in the source.

parts.latex:
Dr Katyal pours $500$ mL of liquid fertiliser into a previously empty bucket. She then fills the bucket with water at a rate of $\dfrac{dV}{dt}$ litres per minute, where $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=\dfrac{5}{t+1}$ and $t$ is time in minutes.

Find the time, to the nearest second, at which there is $10$ L of liquid in the bucket.

solutions.latex:
The volume is the integral of the rate.
$$\begin{aligned} V&=\displaystyle\int\dfrac{5}{t+1}\,dt\\ &=5\ln|t+1|+C \end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $V=0.5$ L.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.5&=5\ln|1|+C\\ C&=0.5 \end{aligned}$$
So $V=5\ln|t+1|+0.5$.

When $V=10$:
$$\begin{aligned} 10&=5\ln|t+1|+0.5\\ \dfrac{9.5}{5}&=\ln|t+1|\\ t+1&=e^{\frac{9.5}{5}}\\ t&=e^{\frac{9.5}{5}}-1\\ &\approx 5.686\text{ min} \end{aligned}$$
This is $5$ min $41$ sec to the nearest second.

$$\therefore\ t=5\text{ min }41\text{ sec}$$
criteria: Finds $C=0.5$ (with $V$ in litres), or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: The integral $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|+C$ is on the reference sheet; $t$ is in minutes.

parts.latex: Show that the derivative of $2x\log_5 x$ is $2\log_5 x+\dfrac{2x}{x\ln5}$
Hence, find $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(\log_5 x+\dfrac{1}{\ln5}\right)dx$.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=\log_5 x\\ u'&=2 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x\ln 5} \end{aligned}$$
Substituting:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(2x\log_5 x\right)&=2\log_5 x+2x\left(\dfrac{1}{x\ln 5}\right)\\ &=2\log_5 x+\dfrac{2x}{x\ln 5} \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Need to show the line of substitution, otherwise it is copying from the answer.

solutions.latex:
From part (a), simplify the derivative:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\log_5 x+\dfrac{2x}{x\ln 5}&=2\log_5 x+\dfrac{2}{\ln 5}\\ &=2\left(\log_5 x+\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\right) \end{aligned}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(\log_5 x+\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\right)dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}2\left(\log_5 x+\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\right)dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\Big[2x\log_5 x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\\ &=\Big[x\log_5 x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \end{aligned}$$
This is undefined, as $\log_5 0$ is undefined.

parts.latex:
Ms Alrubai and Mrs Norman are employed as doctors. They both start on the same annual salary. However, Ms Alrubai negotiated an annual salary increase of $\$5\,000$, while Mrs Norman negotiated an annual salary increase of $7\%$.

Find their starting annual salary given that after $16$ years they have both made the same amount of money in total.

solutions.latex:
Alrubai's salaries form an arithmetic series with $d=5000$. Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{16}&=\dfrac{16}{2}\left[2a+(16-1)5000\right]\\ &=8\left[2a+75\,000\right]\\ &=16a+600\,000 \end{aligned}$$
Norman's salaries form a geometric series with $r=1.07$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{16}&=\dfrac{a\left(1.07^{16}-1\right)}{1.07-1}\\ &=\left(\dfrac{1.07^{16}-1}{0.07}\right)a \end{aligned}$$
Equate the totals and solve for $a$:
$$\begin{aligned} 16a+600\,000&=\left(\dfrac{1.07^{16}-1}{0.07}\right)a\\ \left(16-\dfrac{1.07^{16}-1}{0.07}\right)a&=-600\,000\\ a&=\dfrac{-600\,000}{16-\frac{1.07^{16}-1}{0.07}}\\ &\approx \$50\,470.84 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the starting salary is } \$50\,470.84$$
criteria: Equates the two sums, or equivalent merit
Finds both sums, or equivalent merit
Finds the AP sum $16a+600\,000$, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Most students used the term formula instead of the sum ($-2$); if the term formula is used incorrectly, $-1$.

3560.stem: If Mr Ferrarin wakes up late, the probability that he exercises is $\dfrac{1}{3}$, and if he wakes up on time the probability that he exercises is $\dfrac{4}{5}$.

parts.latex:
In a particular week, Mr Ferrarin wakes up on time on Thursday morning and late on Friday morning.

Find the probability that Mr Ferrarin exercised on at least one of these days.
The probability that Mr Ferrarin wakes up on time on a Monday is $\dfrac{1}{4}$.
Find the probability that Mr Ferrarin exercises on any given Monday.
Hence, or otherwise, find the probability that Mr Ferrarin woke up on time on a Monday, given that he exercised that day.

solutions.latex:
The probability of exercising on at least one day is the complement of exercising on neither day. On time: not exercising is $\dfrac{1}{5}$; late: not exercising is $\dfrac{2}{3}$.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=1-\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\times\dfrac{2}{3}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{13}{15} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the complementary probability, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Add the probabilities of exercising after waking on time and after waking late.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{exercise})&=\dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{4}{5}+\dfrac{3}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{3}\\ &=0.45 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the correct sum of products, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the conditional probability formula, with $A$ = wakes on time and $B$ = exercises:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A|B)&=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}\\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{4}\times\frac{4}{5}}{0.45}\\ &=\dfrac{4}{9} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the conditional probability formula with correct numerator and denominator, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The graphs of $f(x)=-x^2+2$ and $g(x)=x^3-x^2-kx+2$, where $k$ is a constant, are shown below.

The graphs intersect and create two closed regions, A and B.

\exfigure{1338_q33_1}

Show that these two regions have the same area.
can_use: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
The graphs meet where they are equal.
$$\begin{aligned} x^3-x^2-kx+2&=-x^2+2\\ x^3-kx&=0\\ x\left(x^2-k\right)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=\pm\sqrt{k}$.

For region A, $g(x)$ is above $f(x)$, and $g(x)-f(x)=x^3-kx$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\displaystyle\int_{-\sqrt{k}}^{0}\left(x^3-kx\right)dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{kx^2}{2}\right]_{-\sqrt{k}}^{0}\\ &=0-\left(\dfrac{k^2}{4}-\dfrac{k^2}{2}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{k^2}{4} \end{aligned}$$
For region B, $f(x)$ is above $g(x)$, and $f(x)-g(x)=-x^3+kx$.
$$\begin{aligned} B&=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\sqrt{k}}\left(-x^3+kx\right)dx\\ &=\left[-\dfrac{x^4}{4}+\dfrac{kx^2}{2}\right]_{0}^{\sqrt{k}}\\ &=-\dfrac{k^2}{4}+\dfrac{k^2}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{k^2}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=B$$
criteria: Finds both areas, or equivalent merit
Finds one area correctly, or equivalent merit
Finds the intersections $x=0,\pm\sqrt{k}$, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: If an indefinite integral is used, $-1$ (the constant $C$ needs to cancel). If an incorrect intersection is found, carry the error forward.

parts.latex: Find the minimum distance, to the nearest kilometre, between the police and Ned Kelly.

solutions.latex:
After $t$ hours, $HP=20-5t$ and $HN=7t$, with $\angle PHN=120^\circ$.

Applying the cosine rule in triangle $PHN$, $c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C$:
$$\begin{aligned} D^2&=(20-5t)^2+(7t)^2-2(20-5t)(7t)\cos 120^\circ\\ &=400-200t+25t^2+49t^2-2(20-5t)(7t)\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &=400-200t+74t^2+140t-35t^2\\ &=39t^2-60t+400 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes into the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$D$ is a minimum when $D^2$ is, so find the minimum stationary point of $D^2$.
$$\dfrac{d\left(D^2\right)}{dt}=78t-60$$
Stationary point when $78t-60=0$:
$$t=\dfrac{60}{78}=\dfrac{10}{13}$$
Test the sign of the derivative:
$$t=0.7,\ \dfrac{10}{13},\ 0.8:\ \dfrac{d\left(D^2\right)}{dt}=-5.4,\ 0,\ 2.4$$
The gradient changes from negative to positive, so this is a minimum.
$$\begin{aligned} D^2&=39\left(\dfrac{10}{13}\right)^2-60\left(\dfrac{10}{13}\right)+400\\ &\approx 371.5976 \end{aligned}$$
$$D\approx 19.28\text{ km (2 d.p.)}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum distance is about } 19\text{ km}$$
criteria: Finds $t=\dfrac{10}{13}$ and tests for a minimum, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Most students forgot to test to show a minimum, or to use the property of the original function (concave up parabola).
meta.format_note: Question asks for the nearest km; the source gives $D=19.28$ km (2 d.p.), so a final line of 19 km was added from that value.

parts.latex: A series is given as $1-3k+9k^2+\dots$. What is the value of $k$ if the sum to infinity is $\dfrac{3}{4}$?

It is known that $f(x)$ is an odd function and $g(x)$ is an even function.

This matches option A.

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\sqrt{x}\right)$.

solutions.latex:
Write $x\sqrt{x}=x^{\frac{3}{2}}$ and use the power rule.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\sqrt{x}\right)&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)\\&=\dfrac{3}{2}x^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{3\sqrt{x}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, by the product rule, the derivative is $\sqrt{x}+\dfrac{x}{2\sqrt{x}}$.

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\ln\left(\dfrac{1-3x}{1+2x}\right)\right)$.

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws, split the logarithm of a quotient into a difference.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln\left(\dfrac{1-3x}{1+2x}\right)&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\Big[\ln(1-3x)-\ln(1+2x)\Big]\\&=\dfrac{-3}{1-3x}-\dfrac{2}{1+2x}\\&=\dfrac{-3(1+2x)-2(1-3x)}{(1-3x)(1+2x)}\\&=\dfrac{-5}{(1-3x)(1+2x)}\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, by the quotient rule:
$$\dfrac{-5}{(1+2x)^2}\div\dfrac{1-3x}{1+2x}=\dfrac{-5}{(1+2x)(1-3x)}$$
criteria: Splits into a difference of logarithms (or correctly uses the quotient rule), or equivalent merit

figures.cap: Port A, Island B due south, yacht position Y; not to scale

parts.latex: Calculate the distance of the yacht from Island B to the nearest kilometre.
Find the bearing of Island B from the yacht to the nearest degree.

After spending several hours at the island, the speed boat travels due north back to Port A.

How far south of the port will the speed boat be when it is directly west of the yacht?

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1340_q13_s1}

Distance sailed by the yacht: $15\times3=45$ km.

The angle at $A$ between $AB$ (due south) and $AY$ (bearing $120^\circ$) is $180^\circ-120^\circ=60^\circ$.

Applying the cosine rule in triangle $ABY$:
$$\begin{aligned}YB^2&=30^2+45^2-2(30)(45)\cos60^\circ\\&=1575\\YB&=\sqrt{1575}\\&=39.686\ldots\\&\approx40\text{ km}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct cosine rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw: solution diagram for Q13 (key 1340_q13_s1). Triangle ABY: A at top, B due south of A with AB = 30 km, Y on bearing 120 degrees from A with AY = 45 km; north line at A; angle BAY = 60 degrees marked; YB = 40 km (39.7) marked.

solutions.latex:
Applying the sine rule in triangle $ABY$:
$$\dfrac{\sin\angle YBA}{45}=\dfrac{\sin60^\circ}{YB}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned}\sin\angle YBA&=\dfrac{45\sin60^\circ}{YB}\\&=0.98198\ldots\\\angle YBA&=79.1066\ldots^\circ\\&\approx79^\circ\end{aligned}$$
Bearing of $B$ from $Y$:
$$180^\circ+79^\circ=259^\circ\text{T}$$
Using the rounded value $YB=40$ gives $\angle YBA\approx77^\circ$ and bearing $257^\circ\text{T}$. Other methods, such as the cosine rule for the angle at $Y$, also give $259^\circ\text{T}$.
criteria: Correct equation (sine or cosine rule), or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let $x$ be the distance south of the port when the boat is directly west of the yacht. The yacht is 45 km from $A$ on a line making $60^\circ$ with due south.
$$\begin{aligned}\cos60^\circ&=\dfrac{x}{45}\\x&=45\cos60^\circ\\&=22.5\text{ km}\end{aligned}$$
The speed boat is 22.5 km south of the port.

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int 5\sin x\cos^3 x\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Rewrite in the form $\displaystyle\int f'(x)[f(x)]^n\,dx$ with $f(x)=\cos x$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int5\sin x\cos^3x\,dx&=-5\int(-\sin x)\cos^3x\,dx\\&=-5\times\dfrac{\cos^4x}{4}+C\\&=-\dfrac{5\cos^4x}{4}+C\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, let $u=\cos x$, so $du=-\sin x\,dx$:
$$-5\int u^3\,du=-\dfrac{5u^4}{4}+C$$
criteria: Rewrites in the form $\displaystyle\int f'(x)[f(x)]^n\,dx$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the exact gradient of the tangent to the curve $y=x\tan x$ at the point where $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=\tan x\\u'&=1 & v'&=\sec^2x\end{aligned}$$
So
$$y'=\tan x+x\sec^2x$$
At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, $\tan\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$ and $\sec\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}\right)^2\\&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\times\dfrac{4}{3}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}+\dfrac{2\pi}{9}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{gradient}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}+\dfrac{2\pi}{9}$$
criteria: Applies the product rule, or equivalent merit

3580.stem:
Chris and Ann are participating in a charity bicycle ride between Canberra and Liverpool.

Chris leaves Canberra and rides to Liverpool, a distance of 250 km, at an average speed of 20km/h. His distance from Liverpool is modelled by the equation $C=250-20t$, where $C$ is his distance from Liverpool and $t$ is the time in hours he has been riding.

figures.cap: blank grid: distance from Liverpool (km) against time (hours)
solution sketch: graphs of Chris (250-20t) and Ann (90+12t)

parts.latex:
On the grid below, sketch the graph of this model and label it ‘Chris’.

\exfigure{1340_q16_1}

Ann rides in the opposite direction and leaves from Berrima, a town located 90km from Liverpool. She begins riding at the same time as Chris and rides at an average speed of 12km/h towards Canberra.

By drawing a line on the grid above, or otherwise, find the value of $t$ when Chris and Ann pass each other.

parts.latex: Find the value of $t$ when the riders have ridden a total of 264km.

solutions.latex:
The line has $y$-intercept $250$ and gradient $-20$. It meets the $t$-axis when $250-20t=0$, that is at $t=12.5$.

\exfigure{1340_q16_s1}

The part (a) latex used key 1340_q16_s1 while the item sketch_id is 1340_q16_s2; check which key the drawing uses. solutions.latex:
Ann starts 90 km from Liverpool and rides away from it at 12 km/h, so her distance from Liverpool is
$$A=90+12t$$
Chris: $C=250-20t$. They pass each other when $A=C$:
$$\begin{aligned}90+12t&=250-20t\\32t&=160\\t&=5\end{aligned}$$
Graphically, Ann's line from $(0,90)$ with gradient 12 crosses Chris's line at $t=5$.
$$\therefore\ t=5\text{ hours}$$

The distance between them is $A-C$, so set
$$\begin{aligned}90+12t-(250-20t)&=160\\32t-160&=160\\32t&=320\\t&=10\end{aligned}$$
Graphically, at $t=10$ Chris is 50 km and Ann 210 km from Liverpool.
$$\therefore\ t=10\text{ hours}$$

Distance ridden by Chris: $20t$. Distance ridden by Ann: $12t$.
$$\begin{aligned}20t+12t&=264\\32t&=264\\t&=8.25\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=8.25\text{ hours}$$
