3582.stem:
A runner is training for a long-distance event.

The first week she runs 1.2 km.

The second week she runs 1.8 km.

The third week she runs 2.7 km, and so on, adding on half of the previous week.

parts.latex: How far does she run in the fourth week?
How far does she run in \textbf{total} after the first 6 weeks?

The event she is training for is 45 km.

In which week will she first exceed this distance?

solutions.latex:
The common ratio is
$$r=\dfrac{1.8}{1.2}=\dfrac{2.7}{1.8}=1.5$$
Fourth week:
$$T_4=2.7\times1.5=4.05\text{ km}$$
Check: $T_4=1.2\times1.5^3=4.05$ km.

The distances form a geometric series with $a=1.2$, $r=1.5$, $n=6$. Using $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_6&=\dfrac{1.2(1.5^6-1)}{1.5-1}\\&=24.9375\text{ km}\end{aligned}$$
Check by adding the terms: $1.2+1.8+2.7+4.05+6.075+9.1125=24.9375$.
criteria: Correct substitution into the sum formula (or correct terms), or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The $n$th term is $T_n=1.2\times1.5^{n-1}$. Set $T_n=45$:
$$\begin{aligned}45&=1.2\times1.5^{n-1}\\37.5&=1.5^{n-1}\\\ln37.5&=(n-1)\ln1.5\\n&=\dfrac{\ln37.5}{\ln1.5}+1\\&=9.93872\ldots\end{aligned}$$
The terms increase, so the first whole week with $n>9.94$ is week 10.
$$\therefore\ \text{She first exceeds 45 km in the 10th week.}$$

meta.format_note: Source rubric (1 correct equation; 1 for 37.5 = 1.5^(n-1), 1/2 n, 1/2 week) was unclear; rewritten top-down by us.

3583.stem:
Ash and Naomi complete a series of games. The series finishes when one player has won two games.

In any game, the probability that Ash wins is $\dfrac{3}{5}$ and the probability that Naomi wins is $\dfrac{2}{5}$.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=2-1/(x+4)

parts.latex: Draw a probability tree showing the possible outcomes, in a series of three games.
What is the probability that Naomi wins the series?
What is the probability that Naomi wins at least one game?

solutions.latex:
Let $A$ be "Ash wins" and $N$ be "Naomi wins". Each branch has probability $\dfrac{3}{5}$ for $A$ and $\dfrac{2}{5}$ for $N$. After $AA$ or $NN$ the series stops.

\exfigure{1340_q19_s1}
criteria: Correct first two games, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Figure 1340_q19_s1 already referenced; kept. Rubric rewritten top-down.

solutions.latex:
Naomi wins the series by $ANN$, $NAN$ or $NN$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{Naomi wins}) &= P(ANN)+P(NAN)+P(NN) \\ &= 2\times\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\times\dfrac{2}{5}\times\dfrac{2}{5}\right)+\dfrac{2}{5}\times\dfrac{2}{5} \\ &= \dfrac{44}{125} \end{aligned}$$

Naomi wins at least one game unless Ash wins the first two games.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one}) &= 1-P(AA) \\ &= 1-\dfrac{3}{5}\times\dfrac{3}{5} \\ &= \dfrac{16}{25} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Show that $f'(x)=4(x+2)^2(1-x)$.
Find the coordinates of the stationary points of $y=f(x)$ and determine their nature. You may use $f''(x)=-12x(x+2)$.
Find the coordinates of all points of inflection of $y=f(x)$.
Sketch the graph of $y=f(x)$ below, showing all intercepts, stationary points, and points of inflection.
Does $y=f(x)$ have a global maximum or global minimum in its natural domain? If so, specify where.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2-x & v&=(x+2)^3\\ u'&=-1 & v'&=3(x+2)^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= -(x+2)^3+(2-x)\times3(x+2)^2 \\ &= (x+2)^2\left[3(2-x)-(x+2)\right] \\ &= (x+2)^2(6-3x-x-2) \\ &= (x+2)^2(4-4x) \\ &= 4(x+2)^2(1-x) \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Correct use of the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$, so $x=-2$ or $x=1$.
$$f(-2)=0,\quad f(1)=3\times27\div 3\ \text{, that is } f(1)=1\times27=27$$
The points are $(-2,0)$ and $(1,27)$.

Nature of $(1,27)$, using $f''(x)=-12x(x+2)$:
$$f''(1)=-12(1)(3)=-36<0$$
so $(1,27)$ is a maximum turning point.

Nature of $(-2,0)$: here $f''(-2)=0$, so test the concavity either side.
$$\begin{aligned} f''(-3)&=-36 &&\text{concave down}\\ f''(-1)&=12 &&\text{concave up}\end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so $(-2,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflection.
criteria: Finds both stationary points and the nature of one, or equivalent merit
Finds the $x$-values of the stationary points, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source rubric was half-mark steps (both x-values, both y-values, f''(1)<0, maximum, concavity table, inflection statement); rewritten top-down. I tidied the f(1) line: f(1)=(2-1)(3)^3=27.

solutions.latex:
Points of inflection need $f''(x)=0$.
$$-12x(x+2)=0$$
so $x=0$ or $x=-2$.

$$f(0)=2\times8=16$$
From part (b), $(-2,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflection.

Test $(0,16)$ for a change in concavity:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(-1)&=12 &&\text{concave up}\\ f''(1)&=-36 &&\text{concave down}\end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so $(0,16)$ is a point of inflection.

$$\therefore\ \text{points of inflection: } (-2,0) \text{ and } (0,16)$$

meta.format_note: Source rubric was half-mark steps; rewritten top-down.

criteria: Sketch with most features correct, or equivalent merit
Correct intercepts or turning point, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Figure 1340_q20_s1 kept. Source rubric was half-mark steps (x-intercepts -2 and 2, maximum (1,27), horizontal inflection (-2,0), y-intercept 16, smooth shape with both arrows down); rewritten top-down.

solutions.latex:
The curve has a maximum turning point at $(1,27)$ and both ends go down, so there is a global maximum of $27$ when $x=1$.

There is no global minimum, since $y\to-\infty$ as $x\to\pm\infty$.

meta.format_note: Source reason for no global minimum was vague (lowest value cannot be determined); I replaced it with the end behaviour, which both ends going down from the sketch supports. Source rubric half-marks (states global maximum; specifies where) rewritten as single row.

parts.latex: Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_3^4 \dfrac{x}{x^2-8}\,dx$ in simplest form.

solutions.latex:
The numerator is half the derivative of $x^2-8$, so write
$$\begin{aligned} \int_3^4\dfrac{x}{x^2-8}\,dx &= \dfrac12\int_3^4\dfrac{2x}{x^2-8}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac12\Big[\ln|x^2-8|\Big]_3^4 \\ &= \dfrac12\left(\ln8-\ln1\right) \\ &= \dfrac12\ln8 \\ &= \dfrac32\ln2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct antiderivative with the factor $\dfrac12$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the area bounded by the curve, the $x$-axis, and the lines $x=2$ and $x=6$ using the Trapezoidal Rule with five function values. Give your answer correct to three decimal places.

Calculate the same area by evaluating $\displaystyle\int_2^6 \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx$.

Give your answer correct to three decimal places.
Explain why there is a slight difference between your answers in part (a) and part (b).

solutions.latex:
Five function values give $n=4$ strips, so $h=\dfrac{6-2}{4}=1$ and the $x$-values are $2,3,4,5,6$.

Using the trapezoidal rule, $A\approx\dfrac{b-a}{2n}\left\{f(a)+f(b)+2\left[f(x_1)+f(x_2)+f(x_3)\right]\right\}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx \dfrac{6-2}{2\times4}\left\{\dfrac12+\dfrac16+2\left[\dfrac13+\dfrac14+\dfrac15\right]\right\} \\ &\approx 1.117\ \text{units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the $\dfrac{b-a}{2n}$ factor or the correct bracket, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \int_2^6\dfrac1x\,dx &= \Big[\ln|x|\Big]_2^6 \\ &= \ln6-\ln2 \\ &\approx 1.099\ \text{units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

The trapezoidal rule gives an approximation, whereas integration gives the exact area.

The curve is concave up, so the sloping sides of the trapezia lie above the curve and the trapezoidal rule gives an overestimate.

3588.stem:
A particle starts to move from the origin along the $x$-axis.

Its velocity, measured in metres, at some time $t$ seconds, is given by $v=4-\dfrac{2}{3t+1}$ m/s.

parts.latex: Explain why the particle is never at rest.
Find the acceleration of the particle at $t=3$ seconds.
Find the exact distance travelled by the particle between $t=0$ and $t=5$ seconds.
Find the particle’s limiting velocity.

solutions.latex:
If the particle is at rest, $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4-\dfrac{2}{3t+1} &= 0 \\ 4(3t+1) &= 2 \\ 12t &= -2 \\ t &= -\dfrac16 \end{aligned}$$
But $t\ge0$, so the particle is never at rest.

Write $v=4-2(3t+1)^{-1}$ and differentiate.
$$\begin{aligned} a=\dfrac{dv}{dt} &= -2\times(-1)(3t+1)^{-2}\times3 \\ &= \dfrac{6}{(3t+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
When $t=3$:
$$a=\dfrac{6}{(3\times3+1)^2}=\dfrac{6}{100}=0.06\ \text{m/s}^2$$
criteria: Correct expression for $a$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
By part (a) the particle is never at rest and $v>0$, so it never changes direction. The distance equals the displacement.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{distance} &= \int_0^5\left(4-\dfrac{2}{3t+1}\right)dt \\ &= \Big[4t-\dfrac23\ln|3t+1|\Big]_0^5 \\ &= 20-\dfrac23\ln16 \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, $x=4t-\dfrac23\ln|3t+1|+C$, and $x=0$ when $t=0$ gives $C=0$. At $t=5$, $x=20-\dfrac23\ln16$.

$$\therefore\ \text{distance}=\left(20-\dfrac23\ln16\right)\text{ m}$$
criteria: Correct integral set up, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
As $t\to\infty$, $\dfrac{2}{3t+1}\to0$, so $v\to4$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the limiting velocity is } 4 \text{ m/s}$$

At the beginning of the year 1935, 100 cane toads were introduced into Australia. Exactly 5 years later, the population had grown to 1000.

where $N_0$ and $k$ are constants and $t$ is measured in years from the start of 1935.

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\ln(\sec x+\tan x)\right)=\sec x$.
Hence, find the exact area of the shaded region $R$.

solutions.latex:
Apply the chain rule to the logarithm, with $\sec x=(\cos x)^{-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\sec x+\tan x) &= \dfrac{1}{\sec x+\tan x}\times\dfrac{d}{dx}\left((\cos x)^{-1}+\tan x\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sec x+\tan x}\left(\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2x}+\sec^2x\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sec x+\tan x}\left(\tan x\sec x+\sec^2x\right) \\ &= \dfrac{\sec x(\tan x+\sec x)}{\sec x+\tan x} \\ &= \sec x \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Correct derivative of $\sec x+\tan x$ used in the chain rule, or equivalent merit
Applies the chain rule to the logarithm, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The curves meet where $\cos x=\dfrac12\sec x$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\cos x &= \dfrac{1}{\cos x} \\ 2\cos^2x &= 1 \\ \cos^2x &= \dfrac12 \\ \cos x &= \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \end{aligned}$$
The solution in the first quadrant is $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

meta.format_note: Source also listed other solutions $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$, etc. and 'or by substitution'; dropped as not needed.

solutions.latex:
The region lies between $y=\cos x$ (above) and $y=\dfrac12\sec x$ from $x=0$ to $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. Part (a) gives $\displaystyle\int\sec x\,dx=\ln(\sec x+\tan x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} R &= \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\cos x-\dfrac12\sec x\right)dx \\ &= \Big[\sin x-\dfrac12\ln(\sec x+\tan x)\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}-\dfrac12\ln\left(\sqrt2+1\right)\right)-\left(0-\dfrac12\ln1\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}-\dfrac12\ln\left(\sqrt2+1\right)\ \text{units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: piecewise linear graph with points (-6,5), (4,2), (4,-6), (k,-4)

parts.latex:
Use the graph below to find the value of $k$ which satisfies $\displaystyle\int_{-6}^{k} f(x)\,dx=0$.

\exfigure{1340_q27_1}

solutions.latex:
The area above the $x$-axis is a trapezium.
$$A_1=\dfrac12\times10\times(5+2)=35\ \text{units}^2$$
The area below the $x$-axis is a triangle-based region with base $k-4$ and height from the graph.
$$A_2=\dfrac12(k-4)(6+4)=5k-20\ \text{units}^2$$
For $\displaystyle\int_{-6}^{k}f(x)\,dx=0$ the two areas must be equal.
$$\begin{aligned} 5k-20 &= 35 \\ 5k &= 55 \\ k &= 11 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds both areas, or equivalent merit

3592.stem:
Point $A(2e,1)$ lies on the function $h(x)$. The tangent to $h(x)$ at $A$ has equation $y=\dfrac{x}{2e}$.

Point $B$ is the image of the point $A$ on the function $g(x)=3h(2x+4)$.

parts.latex: Show that $B$ has coordinates $(e-2,3)$.
Hence, find the equation of the tangent to $g(x)$ at point $B$, in general form.

solutions.latex:
Write $g(x)=3h\left(2(x+2)\right)$. A point $(x,y)$ on $h$ maps to $\left(\dfrac{x}{2}-2,\,3y\right)$ on $g$.
$$B=\left(\dfrac{2e}{2}-2,\,3\times1\right)=(e-2,\,3)$$

Differentiate $g(x)=3h(2x+4)$ using the chain rule.
$$g'(x)=3h'(2x+4)\times2=6h'(2x+4)$$
At $B$, $x=e-2$, so $2x+4=2e$.
$$g'(e-2)=6h'(2e)$$
But $h'(2e)$ is the gradient of the tangent at $A$, which is $\dfrac{1}{2e}$.
$$g'(e-2)=6\times\dfrac{1}{2e}=\dfrac{3}{e}$$
The tangent at $B$ is
$$\begin{aligned} y-3 &= \dfrac{3}{e}\left(x-(e-2)\right) \\ ey-3e &= 3x-3e+6 \\ 3x-ey+6 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Gradient at $B$ equals $\dfrac{3}{e}$, or equivalent merit
Some correct progress towards the gradient of the tangent to $g(x)$, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: quarter circle radius 5 with points M(2,0), N(0,4), P(x,y), angle theta; not to scale

parts.latex:
Show that the area, $A$, of the quadrilateral $OMPN$ is given by

$$A=5\sin\theta+10\cos\theta$$
Find the value of $\tan\theta$ which gives the maximum area $A$.
Hence find, in surd form, the coordinates of point $P$ when $A$ is maximum.

solutions.latex:
Triangle $OPM$ has $OP=5$ (radius), $OM=2$ and included angle $\theta$.
$$A_{\triangle OPM}=\dfrac12\times5\times2\times\sin\theta=5\sin\theta$$
Triangle $ONP$ has $ON=4$, $OP=5$ and included angle $\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta$.
$$A_{\triangle ONP}=\dfrac12\times4\times5\times\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=10\cos\theta$$
Therefore
$$A=A_{\triangle OPM}+A_{\triangle ONP}=5\sin\theta+10\cos\theta$$
as required.
criteria: Area of one triangle, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $A=5\sin\theta+10\cos\theta$.
$$\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=5\cos\theta-10\sin\theta$$
For a stationary point $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 10\sin\theta &= 5\cos\theta \\ \tan\theta &= \dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
so $\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right)\approx0.463$ radians.

Test the nature:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{d\theta^2}=-5\sin\theta-10\cos\theta\approx-11.18<0$$
so this is a maximum turning point.

$$\therefore\ \text{the maximum area occurs when } \tan\theta=\dfrac12$$
criteria: Solves $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=0$ to get $\tan\theta=\dfrac12$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Since $\tan\theta=\dfrac{y}{x}=\dfrac12$, we have $y=\dfrac{x}{2}$. Also $P$ lies on $x^2+y^2=25$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2+\dfrac{x^2}{4} &= 25 \\ 5x^2 &= 100 \\ x^2 &= 20 \end{aligned}$$
P is in the first quadrant, so $x=2\sqrt5$ and $y=\sqrt5$.

Alternatively, $\sin\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}$ and $\cos\theta=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt5}$, so $y=5\sin\theta=\sqrt5$ and $x=5\cos\theta=2\sqrt5$.

$$\therefore\ P=\left(2\sqrt5,\ \sqrt5\right)$$
criteria: Some correct progress, or equivalent merit
